name: Skill Diagnostic
source: Original difficulty-ladder questions written for LSAT Trainer. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: At the Larkhill Ceramics Studio, any piece that is to be glazed must first be bisque-fired, and no piece is bisque-fired until it has dried on the open shelves for at least a week. Tomas's bowl was glazed at the studio this morning.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Tomas's bowl was bisque-fired at some point within the past week.
Tomas's bowl dried on the studio's open shelves for at least a week.
Every piece that has dried on the open shelves for a week will be bisque-fired.
Any piece at the studio that has been bisque-fired will eventually be glazed.
Tomas's bowl was not glazed on the same day that it was bisque-fired.
questions.explanation: Core move: follow a two-link chain forward from a known fact. Glazed requires bisque-fired, and bisque-fired requires a week on the shelves, so Tomas's glazed bowl must have spent at least a week drying, which is (B). The most tempting traps are (C) and (D), which run the rules backward: drying for a week is required for bisque firing, not a guarantee of it, and being bisque-fired is required for glazing, not a promise of it. (A) and (E) make claims about timing that the rules never fix.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Glazed → bisque-fired first; 2. Bisque-fired → dried on the shelves at least a week; 3. Tomas's bowl was glazed this morning.

breakdown.analysis: Two rules, one fact. Chain them: glazed → bisque-fired → dried a week. Tomas's bowl is glazed, so it rides the whole chain to the end. Prephrase: the bowl was bisque-fired and it dried on the shelves for at least a week. The traps will flip an arrow. 'Must first be' and 'no ... until' both introduce necessary conditions, not guarantees. It's like 'you can't board without a ticket': having a ticket doesn't mean you boarded.

choices.note: We don't know this. The rules say the bowl was bisque-fired before glazing, but not when. It could have been bisque-fired a month ago.
CORRECT. Glazed → bisque-fired → dried at least a week. The bowl was glazed, so it dried for at least a week.

Tempting, because it uses the exact words of rule 2. But it reverses it. A week of drying is needed before bisque firing; it doesn't guarantee a piece gets fired. Some dry pieces may sit on the shelf forever.
This reverses rule 1. Bisque firing is required before glazing, but nothing says every bisque-fired piece gets glazed. Plenty of pottery is left unglazed.
We don't know this. 'Must first be bisque-fired' fixes the order, not the gap between the steps. Same-day is never ruled out.

questions.stimulus: Birding club secretary: A member of our club may lead a field walk only if he or she has completed the club's identification course, and everyone who has completed that course has gone on at least one of the club's night surveys. Any member who has led a field walk is entitled to vote on the club's annual checklist. Corinne, a member, has never gone on a night survey.
questions.stem: If the secretary's statements are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Corinne is not entitled to vote on the club's annual checklist.
Every member who has gone on a night survey has completed the identification course.
Any member who is entitled to vote on the annual checklist has led a field walk.
Corinne has never led one of the club's field walks.
Most members who have completed the identification course have led a field walk.
questions.explanation: Core move: the contrapositive of a chain. Leading a walk requires the course, and the course requires a night survey, so a member with no night survey has not completed the course and cannot have led a walk, which is (D). The tempting trap is (A): it treats 'led a field walk' as the only route to a vote, but the rule only says leading a walk is enough for a vote, so Corinne might qualify some other way. (B) and (C) each reverse one of the rules.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Lead a walk → completed the course; 2. Completed the course → gone on a night survey; 3. Led a walk → may vote on the checklist; 4. Corinne has never gone on a night survey.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: lead a walk → course → night survey. Contrapositive: no night survey → no course → never led a walk. Corinne has no night survey, so she never completed the course and never led a walk. Prephrase: Corinne hasn't led a walk (or hasn't completed the course). The trap is the last rule. Leading a walk gets you a vote, but it's not the only way to get one. Knowing Corinne didn't lead a walk tells you nothing about her vote.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the next step most people take, and it's wrong. 'Led a walk → can vote' gives a sufficient condition. Failing it doesn't block the vote; maybe officers or long-time members can vote too. That's a classic negation error.
This reverses rule 2. Completing the course requires a night survey; it doesn't follow that everyone who went on a night survey took the course.
This reverses rule 3. Leading a walk is enough for a vote, not required for one.
CORRECT. No night survey → no course → no walk. Corinne can't have led a field walk.
We don't know this. The rules say nothing about how many course graduates actually lead walks. It could be none.

questions.stimulus: Library administrator: The board of the Brenton Public Library votes on every program for which the library pays an outside presenter. The board never voted on this summer's astronomy series. So the astronomy series cannot have been eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.
questions.stem: The administrator's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every program for which the library pays an outside presenter is eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.
Most programs that are eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants are voted on by the library's board.
The board votes only on those programs on which the library's rules require it to vote.
No program that the board has voted on has ever received one of the county's arts-partnership grants.
A library program is eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants only if the library pays an outside presenter for it.
questions.explanation: Core move: build the missing link of a chain in the right direction. The premises give 'no board vote → no paid outside presenter' (contrapositive of the first sentence), and the conclusion needs 'no paid outside presenter → not eligible', which is the same as (E): eligible only if there is a paid outside presenter. The most tempting trap is (A), which joins the same two ideas but backward; knowing that paid-presenter programs are eligible says nothing about a program without one. (B) is too weak, since 'most' leaves room for the astronomy series to be an eligible program the board never voted on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The astronomy series was not eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The board votes on every program with a paid outside presenter; the board never voted on the astronomy series.

breakdown.analysis: So the series had no paid outside presenter. Why does that make it ineligible? The argument never says. Chain: paid presenter → board vote. Contrapositive: no board vote → no paid presenter. Conclusion: not eligible. Missing link: no paid presenter → not eligible, which is the same as eligible → paid presenter. Full chain for the series: no vote → no paid presenter → not eligible. Prephrase: 'Only programs with a paid outside presenter are eligible.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the right two ideas. But it points the wrong way: paid presenter → eligible. The series had no paid presenter, so this rule never applies to it.
Too weak. If only most eligible programs get a vote, the series could be one of the eligible programs the board skipped.
Irrelevant. This tells us why the board might skip a program, but nothing about grant eligibility.
Wrong direction. It's about programs the board did vote on. The series wasn't voted on, so this says nothing about it.
CORRECT. Eligible → paid presenter, so no paid presenter → not eligible. The series had no vote, so no paid presenter, so it wasn't eligible.

questions.stimulus: At Bellbrook Hospital, every nurse assigned to the cardiac unit is certified in advanced life support. A nurse who works only night shifts may be assigned to the cardiac unit only if he or she has at least five years of nursing experience. All of the hospital's nurses with five or more years of experience serve on its training rotation, and no one on the training rotation works only night shifts.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: One of the nurses assigned to Bellbrook's cardiac unit works only night shifts.
Some nurse at Bellbrook who is certified in advanced life support works only night shifts.
Some nurse assigned to the cardiac unit has fewer than five years of nursing experience.
Every nurse at Bellbrook who works only night shifts has fewer than five years of experience.
Some nurse on Bellbrook's training rotation is not certified in advanced life support.
questions.explanation: Core move: a chain that loops back and contradicts its own starting point. A night-only nurse in the cardiac unit would need five years' experience, which puts that nurse on the training rotation, and no one on the rotation works only nights, so (A) describes an impossible nurse. The strongest trap is (C), which feels forbidden because of the five-year rule, but that rule applies only to night-only nurses; a day-shift cardiac nurse with two years' experience breaks nothing. (D) is tempting for a different reason: it sounds restrictive, but it actually must be true (five years → rotation → not night-only), and anything that must be true can be true.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Cardiac unit → ALS certified; 2. Night-only AND cardiac unit → 5+ years; 3. 5+ years → training rotation; 4. Training rotation → not night-only.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase a 'cannot be true' from four rules, so look for a chain that runs into a wall. Start with a night-only nurse in the cardiac unit: night-only + cardiac → 5+ years → rotation → NOT night-only. That nurse would have to be both night-only and not night-only. So no night-only nurse is in the cardiac unit. Also note facts 3 and 4 give: night-only → under 5 years. Everything else (ALS certification, day nurses) is loosely tied and can go either way. Watch for answers that sound restrictive but are actually allowed.

choices.note: CORRECT. Night-only + cardiac → 5+ years → rotation → not night-only. Contradiction. This nurse can't exist.
Can be true. ALS certification is required for the cardiac unit, but nothing stops a night-only nurse elsewhere in the hospital from being certified.
Tempting, because the five-year rule is the loudest thing in the stimulus. But it only covers night-only nurses. A day-shift cardiac nurse with two years' experience violates nothing.

Tempting the other way: it sounds like a strong claim, so it feels risky. But it must be true: 5+ years → rotation → not night-only, so every night-only nurse has under five years. Must-be-true answers are never the 'cannot be true' answer.
Can be true. ALS certification is tied to the cardiac unit, not the rotation. A rotation nurse who works outside the cardiac unit needn't be certified.

questions.stimulus: Budget director: Under Rellford's budget policy, any city department that finishes the fiscal year under budget receives a bonus allocation the following year. Critics charge that the parks department's bonus allocation is undeserved, since a department can easily come in under budget by deferring required maintenance. But the city auditor flags every department that defers required maintenance, and the auditor did not flag the parks department. So the parks department's bonus allocation is deserved.
questions.stem: The budget director's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a department finishes the fiscal year under budget by deferring required maintenance, its bonus allocation is undeserved.
Most departments that are not flagged by the city auditor deserve the bonus allocations they receive.
A department's bonus allocation for finishing under budget is undeserved only if the department finished under budget by deferring required maintenance.
No department can finish the fiscal year under budget merely by deferring the maintenance it is required to perform.
Departments that the city auditor does not flag are more likely than flagged departments to have earned their bonus allocations legitimately.
questions.explanation: Core move: proving a positive ('deserved') requires a rule that names deferring maintenance as the only way a bonus can be undeserved. The premises establish that parks did not defer required maintenance (not flagged → didn't defer), and (C), in its contrapositive form, says that a department that didn't finish under budget by deferring maintenance has a bonus that is not undeserved, so the conclusion follows. The trap is (A), which differs from (C) only in 'if' versus 'only if': it states the critics' standard, under which deferring maintenance is one way to make a bonus undeserved, and so it can never show that a bonus is deserved. (B) fails on its quantifier, since parks could be among the unflagged departments whose bonus is undeserved.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The parks department's bonus allocation is deserved.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under budget → bonus; critics: bonus undeserved because a department can come in under budget by deferring maintenance; auditor flags every department that defers required maintenance; parks wasn't flagged.

breakdown.analysis: First, what's proven? Defers → flagged. Contrapositive: not flagged → didn't defer. So parks didn't defer maintenance. Fine. But so what? Ruling out one bad route doesn't prove the bonus is deserved. Maybe parks got under budget by cutting summer programs. The director needs a rule saying deferring maintenance is the ONLY thing that can make a bonus undeserved. Chain: undeserved → got under budget by deferring maintenance. Contrapositive: didn't defer → not undeserved → deserved. Prephrase: 'A bonus is undeserved only if the department deferred maintenance.' Watch 'if' vs 'only if': that one word decides this question.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the critics' own standard, and it sounds like the heart of the dispute. But it runs deferring → undeserved. Parks didn't defer, so this rule is silent about parks. A rule that can only convict can't acquit.
Too weak. 'Most' unflagged departments deserve their bonus; parks could be in the minority that doesn't.
CORRECT. Undeserved → deferred maintenance. Parks didn't defer (not flagged), so its bonus isn't undeserved, which means it's deserved. The awkward 'only if' wording is exactly what makes it work.
So? Even if deferring maintenance couldn't get a department under budget, that only removes one route to an undeserved bonus. It still says nothing about what makes a bonus deserved.
Likelihood isn't proof. 'More likely' can never make a conclusion follow logically, and parks could still be an exception.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: The Pembrook ferry service should replace its diesel boats with electric ones right away. Electric boats are cleaner, quieter, and cheaper to run.

Garrett: Electric boats are certainly cleaner and quieter. But no electric boat now available can make the crossing in a winter storm, so switching now would leave the island cut off for days at a time. The ferry service should wait.
questions.stem: Ines and Garrett disagree over whether
choices: the Pembrook ferry service should replace its diesel boats with electric ones now
electric boats are cleaner and quieter than the ferry service’s diesel boats
electric boats are cheaper to run than the ferry service’s diesel boats
winter storms on the Pembrook crossing are becoming more frequent
island residents would accept being cut off for a few days in exchange for a cleaner ferry
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim one speaker affirms and the other denies. Ines says the service should switch right away; Garrett says it should wait, so they disagree over A. The most tempting trap is C, because cost is one of Ines's reasons; but Garrett never addresses cost, and to disagree, both speakers must take a side. Garrett explicitly agrees with B, and neither speaker addresses D or E.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: Switch to electric boats right away; they're cleaner, quieter, and cheaper to run; Garrett: Granted, cleaner and quieter, but none can cross in a winter storm, so switching now would strand the island; wait.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ines: switch now. Garrett: wait. That's a clean yes/no. Notice what Garrett grants ('certainly cleaner and quieter') and what he skips (cost). Things he grants are agreements; things he skips can't be disagreements.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ines says replace them right away; Garrett says wait. Yes versus no.
They agree. Garrett says electric boats are 'certainly cleaner and quieter.'
Tempting, since cost is one of Ines's reasons. But Garrett never mentions cost. Silence isn't disagreement. You can't disagree about something you never addressed.
Neither speaker says storms are getting more frequent. Garrett only says current electric boats can't handle them.
Neither speaker discusses what residents would accept. Ines doesn't even admit the island would be cut off.

questions.stimulus:
Hanne: Attendance at our community theater has fallen by a fifth this year. We should lower our ticket prices.

Petr: The drop has nothing to do with our prices. The Dorn Playhouse charges even more than we do, and its attendance rose this year.
questions.stem: Petr’s response to Hanne is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that lowering ticket prices would increase the theater’s revenue
draws a conclusion about all theatergoers from a sample of patrons who are unlikely to be representative
attacks Hanne’s motives for proposing lower prices rather than addressing her reasoning
fails to consider that the Dorn Playhouse may differ from Hanne’s theater in ways other than price that affect attendance
takes for granted that the theater’s attendance will continue to fall unless something is changed
questions.explanation: Core move: spot an uneven comparison used to rule out a cause. Petr concludes that price can't explain his theater's decline because a pricier theater did well, but the Dorn Playhouse may have better shows, a better location, or other advantages that outweigh its prices (D). The most tempting trap is A, which describes a weakness in the conversation, but it's Hanne's proposal that relies on lower prices helping, and the question asks about Petr's response. E also describes an assumption Hanne might make, not Petr.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Petr) The attendance drop has nothing to do with prices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Petr) The Dorn Playhouse charges more, and its attendance rose.

breakdown.analysis: So the Dorn charges more and is doing fine. Does that prove price doesn't matter here? Only if the two theaters are alike in every other way. Maybe the Dorn has bigger stars, a downtown location, or a hit show. Then price could still be hurting Hanne's theater; the Dorn just has something that outweighs it. It's like saying 'that restaurant is pricier than ours and packed, so our prices can't be why we're empty,' when that restaurant has a famous chef. We need an answer that says Petr ignores other differences between the theaters.

choices.note: Tempting, because something like this is a fair question to ask in this conversation. But it's about Hanne's proposal. Petr never says anything about revenue. Read the stem: it asks about Petr's response.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should cut our prices in half; that will obviously bring in more money.

choices.note: No sample of theatergoers is involved. Petr compares two theaters.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The five patrons I asked at opening night said prices are fine, so no one in town thinks our prices are too high.

choices.note: Petr never mentions Hanne's motives. He addresses her claim directly.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Hanne only wants lower prices because her friends would get in cheaper, so we can ignore her.

choices.note: CORRECT. Petr uses one pricier theater's success to rule out price as a cause, without considering that the Dorn may have other advantages, like better shows or location, that more than offset its prices.
Petr doesn't predict anything about future attendance. If anyone assumes the drop will continue, it's Hanne.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Attendance fell this year, so it will keep falling every year unless we act.

questions.stimulus:
Lucia: The Hollin Seed Bank should let home gardeners borrow seed of its rare varieties. If gardeners keep those varieties growing, the varieties will survive even if the bank’s freezers someday fail.

Arno: Having rare varieties grown outside the vault is certainly worthwhile. But gardeners’ plants will cross-pollinate with nearby plants, so any seed they return would no longer be true to type. The bank should instead pay a few trained growers to raise rare varieties in isolated plots.
questions.stem: Lucia and Arno are committed to agreeing that
choices: seed returned to the seed bank by home gardeners would not be true to type
the seed bank’s freezers are likely to fail at some point
the seed bank should arrange for at least some rare varieties to be grown outside its vault
trained growers would keep rare varieties true to type more reliably than home gardeners would
preserving rare varieties is the most important function of the seed bank
questions.explanation: Core move: for agreement, each speaker must be committed to the claim, not merely not deny it. Lucia's plan has gardeners growing rare varieties and Arno's has trained growers doing so, and Arno calls outside growing 'worthwhile,' so both are committed to C. The most tempting trap is D, which Arno clearly believes, but Lucia says nothing about trained growers or seed purity. B overreads Lucia's 'even if … someday,' which is a hedge, not a prediction, and A is Arno's objection, which Lucia never accepts.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Lucia: Lend rare-variety seed to home gardeners so the varieties survive even if the freezers fail; Arno: Outside growing is worthwhile, but gardeners' plants will cross-pollinate; pay trained growers to raise them in isolated plots instead.

breakdown.analysis: They disagree on WHO should grow the rare varieties. But both plans have the varieties grown outside the vault, and Arno says outright that's worthwhile. Agreement questions punish answers only one speaker holds. Test each choice: would Lucia sign it? Would Arno? Both must say yes.

choices.note: Only Arno. This is his objection to Lucia's plan, and she never accepts it.
Neither commits to this. Lucia says 'even if the freezers someday fail,' which is a precaution, not a prediction.
CORRECT. Lucia's plan has gardeners grow them; Arno's has trained growers grow them. Different methods, same goal: rare varieties grown outside the vault.
Tempting. Arno clearly believes this; it's his whole reason for preferring trained growers. But Lucia never mentions trained growers or seed purity. One speaker's view isn't agreement.
Too strong. Neither speaker ranks the seed bank's functions.

questions.stimulus:
Odile: The Marsh Lane weaving mill’s new dye cannot be what has been turning the Fennick River cloudy. The mill uses that dye only on days when it runs a second shift, and the river has turned cloudy on several days when no second shift was run.

Bastien: Your argument assumes that the dye could affect the river only on the days it is used. But the mill collects its rinse water in holding ponds and releases it into the river once a week, regardless of which shifts have been run.
questions.stem: Bastien responds to Odile’s argument by
choices: asserting that the mill’s new dye is in fact what has been turning the river cloudy
identifying a way the dye could cloud the river on days when it is not used, thereby undercutting the inference Odile draws from her evidence
disputing Odile’s claim that the mill uses the new dye only on days when it runs a second shift
charging that Odile treats a condition that is necessary for the river’s cloudiness as though it were sufficient for it
suggesting that the river’s cloudiness on certain days was caused by something other than the mill’s operations
questions.explanation: Core move: describe a reply that attacks an assumption rather than the conclusion. Odile infers that the dye isn't the cause because the river clouded on days the dye wasn't used; Bastien shows how the dye could still reach the river on those days, through the weekly release from the holding ponds, so her evidence no longer rules the dye out (B). The strongest trap is A, which treats Bastien as arguing the dye is the culprit; he never says it is, only that Odile's evidence doesn't clear it. D sounds technical and plausible, but Bastien's point is about timing, not about confusing necessary and sufficient conditions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Odile) The new dye can't be what is clouding the river.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Odile) Dye used only on second-shift days; river cloudy on days with no second shift. (Bastien) You assume the dye acts only on days it's used; rinse water is held in ponds and released weekly no matter which shifts ran.

breakdown.analysis: Odile's logic: if the dye caused it, the river would be cloudy only on dye days. Cloudy on non-dye days, so not the dye. Bastien goes after the 'only on dye days' assumption: the dye sits in ponds and gets released later. So cloudiness on a non-dye day is no evidence against the dye. Does he say the dye IS the cause? No. He just takes away Odile's reason for clearing it. It's like saying 'the cake can't have made me sick, because I got sick on a day I didn't eat any,' and a friend pointing out you ate leftovers of it.

choices.note: Tempting. Bastien sounds like he suspects the dye, and he might. But he never claims it IS the cause. He only shows Odile's evidence doesn't clear it. Undercutting an argument isn't proving its opposite.
choices.example: Example of method: Water samples taken on every cloudy day contained the new dye, so the dye is what's clouding the river.

choices.note: CORRECT. The holding ponds give the dye a path into the river on days it isn't used. That defeats Odile's inference without asserting the opposite conclusion.
No. Bastien accepts that the dye is used only on second-shift days. His point is about when it reaches the river.
choices.example: Example of method: Actually, the mill uses that dye on most weekdays, whether or not a second shift runs.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the kind of thing a sharp critic says. But Bastien's point is about timing, a delayed release. He doesn't accuse Odile of reversing a conditional.
choices.example: Example of method: You show the dye must be present for the river to cloud, but that doesn't mean the dye alone is enough to cloud it.

choices.note: Opposite direction. Bastien's point keeps the mill in the picture; he doesn't offer a non-mill cause.
choices.example: Example of method: The cloudiness on those days came from runoff after heavy rain upstream, not from anything the mill did.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: The junior chess program at the Tarrow library has clearly raised its participants’ math grades. Children who joined the program last fall improved their math grades this year by more than their classmates who did not join.

Priya: Joining the program may well improve children’s math grades, but your evidence doesn’t show it. The parents who enroll their children in an after-school chess program are also the parents most likely to be pushing them in math. So the gap you describe could exist even if the program did nothing.
questions.stem: Hollis and Priya disagree over whether
choices: the junior chess program raised the math grades of the children who joined it
children who joined the program improved their math grades more than their classmates who did not
parents who enroll their children in after-school chess programs tend to push them in math
after-school chess programs generally improve children’s performance in school
the difference in math improvement between the program’s participants and their classmates establishes that the program raised participants’ grades
questions.explanation: Core move: separate disagreement about a conclusion from disagreement about whether the evidence proves it. Hollis says the improvement gap shows the program raised grades; Priya says the gap doesn't show that, since it could exist even if the program did nothing, so they disagree over E. The most tempting trap is A, which differs from E only in dropping 'establishes'; Priya explicitly allows that the program 'may well' improve grades, so she doesn't deny that it did. B is a fact Priya accepts, and C is asserted only by Priya.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hollis: The program clearly raised math grades, because participants improved more than classmates; Priya: It may well help, but the evidence doesn't show it: pushy parents could explain the gap even if the program did nothing.

breakdown.analysis: Does Priya say the program didn't work? No: 'may well improve.' She says the evidence doesn't prove it. So the fight isn't over whether the program works; it's over whether this gap proves it works. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. On 'did the program raise grades?' Hollis says yes and Priya says maybe. Maybe isn't no. On 'does the gap prove it?' Hollis says yes and Priya says no. This is the classic split between a conclusion and the support for it. Know it.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the trap built for this question. Hollis says yes. But Priya says the program 'may well' improve grades. She never says it didn't. 'Not proven' isn't 'false.' Without a 'no' from Priya, there's no disagreement.
They agree, or at least Priya accepts it. She calls it 'the gap you describe' and explains it; she never disputes it.
Only Priya says this. Hollis never mentions parents.
Too broad. Both speakers discuss one program at one library, and neither talks about school performance in general.

CORRECT. Hollis treats the gap as proof ('clearly raised'). Priya says it doesn't show that, because the gap could exist even if the program did nothing. Yes versus no on whether the evidence establishes the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Councillor Brandt: The engineering consultant who recommends that Port Sallow build a seawall along its harbor stands to gain from that recommendation, since her firm would be hired to design the wall if it were built. We should therefore reject her conclusion that a seawall is the best way to protect the harbor from storm surges.
questions.stem: The reasoning in Councillor Brandt's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that a seawall would cost more than other forms of storm protection
overlooks the possibility that the consultant's firm could also profit from other kinds of storm-protection projects
takes for granted that storm surges pose a serious threat to Port Sallow's harbor
rejects a conclusion because of the circumstances of the person who advanced it rather than on its merits
relies on the opinion of an expert whose expertise lies outside the field under discussion
questions.explanation: Core move: spot an attack on the source (ad hominem) in its quietest form, a possible motive. Brandt never touches the consultant's reasons; he rejects her conclusion only because her firm would profit, which is what (D) says. A person with a stake in a recommendation can still be right. The most tempting trap is (E), because the argument is about an expert, but Brandt doesn't rely on anyone's opinion at all; he dismisses one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Port Sallow should reject the consultant's conclusion that a seawall is the best protection against storm surges.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her firm would be hired to design the wall if it were built, so she stands to gain from the recommendation.

breakdown.analysis: So what if she'd profit? Profit gives her a reason to say it, but it doesn't make it false. Brandt never looks at her evidence about surges or seawalls. He just points at her paycheck. It's like ignoring your dentist's advice to fix a cavity because the dentist gets paid for fillings; the cavity is still there. This is ad hominem (the circumstantial kind). It's a classic; know it. Prephrase: attacks the person's motive instead of the recommendation.

choices.note: Cost never comes up. Brandt's only reason is the consultant's stake, so the argument presumes nothing about price.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should build a seawall rather than restore the dunes, since a seawall is obviously the cheaper choice.

choices.note: So? Whether her firm could profit elsewhere doesn't change what Brandt's argument does wrong. The flaw is dismissing her conclusion because of a motive, not miscounting her motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The consultant gains only if a seawall is built, so she has no reason to favor dune restoration, ignoring that her firm might be hired for that too.

choices.note: Brandt doesn't take this for granted; he says nothing about how serious the surges are. And the consultant's claim is about the best protection, which Brandt rejects on other grounds.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We must build a seawall at once, since storm surges are obviously the biggest danger the harbor faces.

choices.note: CORRECT. Brandt's only reason for rejecting the recommendation is the consultant's personal stake in it. That says nothing about whether a seawall really is the best protection.
Tempting, because the argument is about an expert. But Brandt doesn't rely on anyone's expertise. He rejects an expert's view; he doesn't lean on an off-topic one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous novelist says a seawall is the best defense against storm surges, so the council should build one.

questions.stimulus: Dairy farmer: Last spring we installed motorized grooming brushes in our barn, which the cows can use to scratch themselves whenever they like. Over the following six months, our herd's average daily milk yield was 7 percent higher than in the six months before. Clearly, the brushes are responsible for the increase, so we should keep them running rather than shut them off to save on electricity.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the dairy farmer's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about dairy cows from the experience of a single herd
fails to consider that the herd's milk yield might have risen over that period even without the brushes
presumes, without providing justification, that saving on electricity is the farm's most important goal
takes for granted that the cows that used the brushes enjoyed using them
confuses a condition that is required for a high milk yield with one that guarantees it
questions.explanation: Core move: a before/after change treated as proof of cause. The farmer compares spring-and-summer yield with the previous autumn-and-winter yield and credits the brushes, without asking whether yield would have risen anyway (season, feed, pasture), which is (B). The most tempting trap is (A), a sampling flaw, but the farmer draws no conclusion about dairy cows in general; both claims are about this herd. (C) gets the argument backward: the farmer puts the brushes ahead of electricity savings.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brushes caused the rise in milk yield, so the farm should keep them running.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brushes went in last spring; average daily yield in the next six months was 7 percent higher than in the previous six.

breakdown.analysis: Is the brush the only thing that changed between those two six-month stretches? Look at the calendar. The 'after' period is spring and summer; the 'before' period is autumn and winter. Fresh pasture, longer days, new calves: lots of things could lift yield. It's like buying a new umbrella in April and crediting it for the sunny weather in June. Prephrase: the argument ignores other causes; yield might have risen anyway.

choices.note: Tempting, because one herd is a small sample. But the farmer never generalizes. Both the causal claim and the plan are about this herd only.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our herd gave more milk after we installed brushes, so brushes will raise yield on dairy farms everywhere.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument treats 'yield went up after the brushes' as 'the brushes raised yield.' If yield would have risen over spring and summer anyway, the brushes may have done nothing.
This is backward. The farmer explicitly ranks the brushes above the electricity savings. Nothing presumes saving power is the top goal.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should switch off every machine in the barn at night, since cutting the electric bill matters more than anything else on the farm.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the cows enjoyed the brushes doesn't matter to the argument, which rests on the yield numbers, and the farmer never assumes it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The cows crowd around the brushes, so they must enjoy them, and anything they enjoy must be good for them.

choices.note: There is no conditional here. The farmer doesn't say the brushes are required for, or guarantee, high yield; the claim is a simple causal one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Well-fed cows are needed for a high yield, and our cows are well fed, so our herd will have a high yield.

questions.stimulus: Choir director: Any singer who passes our sight-reading audition is guaranteed a place in the chamber choir. Marisol has a place in the chamber choir this season, so she must have passed the sight-reading audition. And since Teodor did not pass that audition, he cannot have a place in the chamber choir.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the choir director's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats a requirement for joining the chamber choir as though it were enough to guarantee a place in it
overlooks the possibility that some singers who pass the audition may decline a place in the chamber choir
draws a conclusion about every member of the chamber choir based on only two cases
presumes, without justification, that the sight-reading audition accurately measures a singer's ability
treats a condition that guarantees a place in the chamber choir as though every singer with a place must have met it
questions.explanation: Core move: sufficient vs. necessary, and noticing which direction the mistake runs. Passing the audition is enough for a place (pass → place), but the director treats it as required (place → pass, and no pass → no place); there could be other routes in, such as a returning-member invitation. (E) states exactly that error. The most tempting trap is (A), which names the same pair of ideas but reversed: it accuses the director of treating a requirement as a guarantee, which is the opposite of what the director does.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marisol must have passed the audition, and Teodor, who didn't pass, can't be in the chamber choir.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pass the sight-reading audition → guaranteed a place in the chamber choir.

breakdown.analysis: The rule: pass → place. That tells you passing is one way in. Is it the only way? The director acts as if it is. Marisol: place → pass. That reverses the arrow. Teodor: no pass → no place. That negates both sides. Both moves only work if passing is required, and the rule never says that. It's like saying anyone who wins the lottery can afford a boat, so your neighbor with a boat must have won the lottery. Prephrase: treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the right vocabulary. But it's the reverse error. The premise is a guarantee, and the director treats it as a requirement, not the other way around.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Only singers who pass the audition can join the chamber choir. Lina passed, so she must have a place in it.

choices.note: So? Someone declining a place would not rescue either conclusion. Marisol has a place, and the question is how she got it; Teodor didn't pass at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every singer who passed the audition was offered a place, so every one of them is singing in the chamber choir this season.

choices.note: The director draws conclusions only about Marisol and Teodor, not about the whole choir. There's no generalization here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Marisol and Teodor both passed the audition before joining, so every chamber choir member must have passed it.

choices.note: The audition's accuracy doesn't matter. Even a perfect audition would leave open other routes into the choir.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Teodor scored poorly on the sight-reading audition, so he must be a weak singer overall.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passing guarantees a place; it isn't shown to be the only way to get one. The director assumes every member passed (Marisol) and that failing keeps you out (Teodor).

questions.stimulus: Warehouse operations manager: Since we installed the automated conveyor system at our Dunmore warehouse, some workers have complained that more of them are getting hurt on the job than before. That complaint is mistaken. In each of the five years before the installation, about 6 percent of our warehouse workers suffered an on-the-job injury, but last year, the first full year with the conveyors, only 4 percent did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the manager's reasoning?
choices: It infers that fewer workers were injured from evidence that a smaller proportion of workers were injured.
It fails to consider that the injuries suffered last year may have been more serious, on average, than those suffered before the installation.
It draws a conclusion about the conveyor system's long-term safety from a single year of data.
It presumes, without providing justification, that the conveyor system was responsible for the drop in the injury rate.
It dismisses the workers' complaint on the grounds that the workers have a motive for exaggerating the danger.
questions.explanation: Core move: rate vs. number. The workers complained that more of them are getting hurt, a claim about a count, and the manager answers with a percentage; if the warehouse hired many more workers to run the conveyors, 4 percent of the larger staff could be more people than 6 percent of the old one, so (A) is the flaw. The most tempting trap is (B), because severity is a classic gap in injury arguments, but the complaint and the rebuttal are both about how many workers were hurt, not how badly. (D) fails because the manager never claims the conveyors lowered the rate; he only says the complaint is false.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The workers' complaint that more of them are getting hurt than before is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Before the conveyors, about 6 percent of workers were injured each year; last year, 4 percent were.

breakdown.analysis: Read the complaint exactly: 'more of them are getting hurt.' That's a number of people. The manager answers with a percentage. Percentages need a base. Imagine 200 workers before: 6 percent is 12 people. If the conveyors brought the staff to 400, 4 percent is 16 people. More workers hurt, lower rate. This is percent vs. number. It's everywhere on the LSAT; know it. Prephrase: a lower injury rate doesn't show fewer injured workers if the workforce grew.

choices.note: CORRECT. The complaint is about how many workers get hurt. A drop from 6 to 4 percent shows that only if the size of the workforce didn't grow enough to offset it.

Tempting. Severity is a real gap in many injury arguments. But here the complaint is 'more of them are getting hurt,' a head count, and the manager's answer is about a head count too. How serious the injuries were doesn't bear on that.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We had fewer injuries this year than last, so this year was safer, even though this year's injuries included two broken backs.

choices.note: The manager draws no long-term conclusion. The claim is only that the complaint about last year's injuries is wrong.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell in the first year after the conveyors went in, so the conveyors will keep the warehouse safe for decades.

choices.note: The manager never credits the conveyors with the drop. He only says the complaint is false. Whether the system caused the change isn't part of the argument.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell after we installed the conveyors, so the conveyors must be what made the warehouse safer.

choices.note: The manager doesn't mention the workers' motives at all. He answers with numbers, flawed as that answer is.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The workers just want hazard pay, so we can ignore their claim that the conveyors are dangerous.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: Under our agency's standard, a windstorm counts as a derecho only if it produces damaging winds along a path at least 400 kilometers long. Some residents insist that last week's storm was a derecho, and admittedly it was violent: our survey teams confirmed toppled trees and roof damage at sites along a 260-kilometer stretch of the river valley. But the teams confirmed no damage beyond that stretch. So the storm's damage path fell well short of 400 kilometers, and the storm was not a derecho.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the meteorologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a condition that is required for a storm to be classified as a derecho as if it were enough to make a storm one
presumes that the survey teams confirmed every instance of damage that the storm caused within the 260-kilometer stretch
presumes that the storm produced no damaging winds at any location where the survey teams did not confirm damage
rejects the residents' view solely because the residents lack expertise in classifying storms
overlooks the possibility that some of the damage the teams confirmed was caused by something other than the storm's winds
questions.explanation: Core move: lack of evidence treated as evidence of absence, hidden inside valid conditional logic. The 'only if' rule is used correctly (path under 400 km → not a derecho); the gap is the step from 'the teams confirmed no damage beyond 260 km' to 'there was no damage beyond 260 km,' which (C) names in indirect form. The most tempting trap is (B), which sounds almost the same but concerns damage inside the stretch; missing sites there can't change the path's length, so the argument doesn't need that presumption. (A) tempts students who see 'only if' and assume a conditional error, but the meteorologist never treats the 400-km condition as sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Last week's storm was not a derecho.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Derecho → damage path of at least 400 km; teams confirmed damage along 260 km; they confirmed none beyond that; so the path was under 400 km (intermediate conclusion).

breakdown.analysis: First, check the formal logic, because that's where you'll be tempted to pounce. Derecho → 400+ km path. Contrapositive: under 400 km → not a derecho. The meteorologist uses it correctly. So the problem is earlier: how do we know the path was under 400 km? Because the teams 'confirmed no damage beyond that stretch.' Did they look beyond it? Were there sites to see? Not finding damage isn't the same as there being none. It's like saying a book has no typos past page 260 because the proofreader found none there, when she may have stopped reading at page 260. Prephrase: assumes that unconfirmed damage didn't happen.

choices.note: Tempting if you see 'only if' and assume the usual error. But the argument uses the rule in its valid contrapositive form: path too short → not a derecho. It never says 400 km is enough to make one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A storm is a derecho only if its damage path is at least 400 kilometers. This storm's path was 450 kilometers, so it was a derecho.

choices.note: Tempting, and it differs from the right answer by one idea: 'within' the stretch. Missed damage inside the 260 km doesn't change the path's length, so the argument needn't presume the teams caught all of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The teams found damage at forty sites in the valley, so the storm must have damaged exactly forty sites there.

choices.note: CORRECT. The step from 'no confirmed damage beyond 260 km' to 'the path fell short of 400 km' works only if the storm caused no damage wherever the teams didn't confirm any. That is treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence.
The meteorologist never mentions the residents' expertise. The residents' view is rejected on the basis of the survey data, not their credentials.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The residents aren't trained meteorologists, so their claim that the storm was a derecho must be wrong.

choices.note: This would actually help the meteorologist: if some confirmed damage wasn't caused by the storm, the path is even shorter. A flaw has to be something that leaves the conclusion unsupported.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The storm damaged homes along a 260-kilometer path, so it caused every broken window reported in the valley that week.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Since beavers returned to Pike Creek five years ago, the number of young salmon in the creek has doubled. Beaver dams create deep, slow pools in which young salmon can shelter from predators. So the beavers' return is responsible for the increase in young salmon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ecologist's argument depends?
choices: Before the beavers returned, young salmon in Pike Creek were more exposed to predators than young salmon in other creeks were.
Young salmon in creeks without beavers rarely survive long enough to reach the sea.
Beaver dams are the only source of deep, slow pools anywhere in Pike Creek.
The increase in young salmon in Pike Creek is not mainly due to some change in the creek other than the beavers' return.
The number of young salmon in Pike Creek will keep rising for as long as the beavers remain there.
questions.explanation: Core move: a causal conclusion drawn from a before-and-after change assumes no other change did the work. If some other change, such as cleaner water or reduced fishing, mainly produced the increase, the beavers would not be responsible, so the argument requires (D). The tempting trap is (C): it seems to make the beavers indispensable, but the argument doesn't need them to be the only source of pools; negate it and the beaver pools can still have doubled the salmon. (B) is likewise too strong and about other creeks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The beavers' return caused the doubling of young salmon in Pike Creek.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The salmon doubled after the beavers returned; beaver dams make pools where young salmon hide from predators.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after. But what else changed in five years? Maybe a factory upstream closed, or fishing was banned. When an argument says 'X happened, then Y went up, so X caused Y', it assumes nothing else caused Y. Prephrase: 'Some other change didn't cause the increase.' It's like crediting your new running shoes for a faster mile when you also quit smoking the same month.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Other creeks don't matter. Negate it (salmon here were no more exposed than elsewhere) and beavers could still have doubled them here.
choices.negation: Before the beavers returned, young salmon in Pike Creek were no more exposed to predators than young salmon in other creeks were.

choices.note: Too strong, and about other creeks. Negate it (young salmon in beaver-free creeks often survive) and Pike Creek's beavers could still be the reason for this increase.
choices.negation: Young salmon in creeks without beavers do not rarely survive long enough to reach the sea.

choices.note: Tempting: it makes the beavers seem essential. But the argument doesn't need beaver pools to be the only pools. Negate it (there are some other pools too) and the new beaver pools can still explain the doubling.
choices.negation: Beaver dams are not the only source of deep, slow pools in Pike Creek.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the increase is mainly due to some other change. Then the beavers aren't responsible, and the argument falls apart.
choices.negation: The increase in young salmon in Pike Creek is mainly due to some change in the creek other than the beavers' return.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument explains the past increase; it predicts nothing. Negate it (the numbers will level off) and the conclusion is untouched.
choices.negation: The number of young salmon in Pike Creek will not keep rising for as long as the beavers remain there.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Patients who miss appointments at our outpatient clinics most often tell us that they simply forgot. So our plan to send appointment reminders through the hospital's new mobile app should substantially reduce the number of missed appointments.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the administrator's argument?
choices: Every patient who forgets an appointment owns a smartphone that can run the hospital's app.
Many of the patients who would otherwise forget their appointments will receive the reminders the app sends.
Reminders sent through the app will be more effective than reminders sent by ordinary text message.
Patients who miss appointments are no more likely than other patients to have serious health problems.
Forgetting is the only reason that patients miss appointments at the hospital's outpatient clinics.
questions.explanation: Core move: a plan that works through a channel assumes the channel reaches the people it targets. The reminders can only help patients who get them, so if few forgetful patients use the app, the plan can't substantially reduce missed appointments; that's (B). The tempting trap is (A), which points at the same worry but is too strong: the plan can work even if some forgetful patients lack smartphones. (E) is also too strong, since the stimulus says forgetting is the most common reason, and the plan only needs to cut that one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Sending reminders through the new app will substantially reduce missed appointments.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Patients who miss appointments most often say they forgot.

breakdown.analysis: Reminders fix forgetting. Fine. But only if the forgetful patients actually get them. A brand-new app: who has it installed? If the forgetful patients mostly don't use it, the reminders go nowhere. Prephrase: 'A good number of the forgetful patients will get the app's reminders.' It's like putting a 'Wet Paint' sign in a room nobody walks into.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the right worry. But 'every' is too strong. Negate it (some forgetful patients don't have a capable phone) and the plan can still reach most of them.
choices.negation: At least one patient who forgets an appointment does not own a smartphone that can run the hospital's app.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: few forgetful patients will receive the reminders. Then the reminders can't make a substantial dent, and the plan fails.
choices.negation: Few of the patients who would otherwise forget their appointments will receive the reminders the app sends.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. The plan only needs to work, not to beat text messages. Negate it and the app reminders can still substantially help.
choices.negation: Reminders sent through the app will not be more effective than reminders sent by ordinary text message.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Health status doesn't affect whether reminders cure forgetting. Negate it and the argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: Patients who miss appointments are more likely than other patients to have serious health problems.

choices.note: Too strong. The stimulus says forgetting is the most common reason, not the only one. Fixing the most common cause can be enough. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Forgetting is not the only reason that patients miss appointments at the hospital's outpatient clinics.

questions.stimulus: Budget analyst: Fuel accounts for 40 percent of the cost of operating our city's fleet of garbage trucks. The electric garbage trucks the city is considering use no fuel at all. So replacing our diesel trucks with electric ones would substantially reduce the cost of operating the fleet.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the budget analyst's argument depends?
choices: Electric garbage trucks cost no more to purchase than the diesel garbage trucks the city now uses.
Electric garbage trucks require less maintenance than diesel garbage trucks do.
The price of diesel fuel in the region is likely to rise steadily over the next several years.
Most cities that have already switched to electric garbage trucks are satisfied with their performance.
The fleet's other operating costs, electricity included, would not rise by nearly as much as the savings on fuel.
questions.explanation: Core move: removing one 40 percent slice of a cost only lowers the total if the other slices don't grow to fill the hole. Electric trucks skip fuel but need electricity and may cost more in other ways; if those increases nearly match the fuel savings, there is no substantial reduction, so the argument needs (E). The most tempting trap is (A), which raises a real money worry but concerns purchase price, while the conclusion is about operating cost. (B) is also attractive but too strong: maintenance could stay the same and the fuel savings alone would still cut costs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching to electric garbage trucks would substantially reduce the fleet's operating cost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fuel is 40 percent of operating cost; electric trucks use no fuel.

breakdown.analysis: No fuel. Great. But do electric trucks run on air? Electricity costs money, and maybe batteries or repairs cost more too. Cutting a 40 percent slice only shrinks the pie if the other slices don't swell. Prephrase: 'The new costs won't come close to eating up the fuel savings.' And note the dimension: the conclusion is about operating cost, not purchase price.

choices.note: Tempting: price matters to a budget analyst. But the conclusion is about operating cost, not buying cost. Negate it (electric trucks cost more to buy) and operating costs could still fall.
choices.negation: Electric garbage trucks cost more to purchase than the diesel garbage trucks the city now uses.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. The argument doesn't need maintenance savings. Negate it (maintenance costs the same) and the fuel savings alone still cut the bill.
choices.negation: Electric garbage trucks do not require less maintenance than diesel garbage trucks do.

choices.note: Strengthens a bit, but isn't required. Negate it (fuel prices stay flat) and fuel is still 40 percent of costs that electric trucks avoid.
choices.negation: The price of diesel fuel in the region is not likely to rise steadily over the next several years.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other cities' satisfaction isn't this city's operating cost. Negation does nothing to the argument.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most cities that have already switched to electric garbage trucks are satisfied with their performance.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: other costs, electricity included, would rise by nearly as much as the fuel savings, or more. Then there's no substantial reduction, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: The fleet's other operating costs, electricity included, would rise by nearly as much as the savings on fuel, or by more.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Opponents of the self-checkout kiosks installed at the Wexley Public Library last year point out that, since then, the share of the library's loans going to patrons over sixty-five has fallen from 30 percent to 22 percent. They conclude that the kiosks have discouraged older patrons from borrowing. But the kiosks arrived at the same time as our new children's reading program, which has sharply increased the number of loans to children. So the drop in that share does not show that older patrons are borrowing any less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the board member's argument?
choices: The number of loans to patrons over sixty-five has not declined at all since the kiosks were installed.
Patrons over sixty-five find the self-checkout kiosks no harder to use than younger patrons do.
The rise in loans to children has not been largely offset by fewer loans to patrons who are neither children nor over sixty-five.
Few patrons over sixty-five take part in the library's new children's reading program.
Before the kiosks were installed, patrons over sixty-five accounted for a larger share of loans than any other age group did.
questions.explanation: Core move: a share can fall because the other slices grew, but only if the total actually grew. The board member explains the drop by the surge in children's loans; if that surge were cancelled out by fewer loans to other adults, total loans would be flat, and a share falling from 30 to 22 percent would mean older patrons really are borrowing less, so the argument requires (C). The strongest trap is (A), which sounds like what the board member believes, but the conclusion is only that the statistic doesn't show a decline; a small real decline is compatible with it. (B) tempts by echoing the opponents' story, but the board member's rebuttal is purely about the numbers, not about how easy the kiosks are.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in the share of loans to patrons over 65 doesn't show they're borrowing less.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Opponents: the over-65 share fell from 30% to 22%, so the kiosks drove older patrons away; reply: children's loans rose sharply at the same time.

breakdown.analysis: Percent vs. number: know this one. A share can shrink while the count stays put if the total grows. Say older patrons borrowed 30 of 100 loans. If the total rises to about 136, the same 30 loans are only 22%. The board member's story needs the total to have actually grown. But what if children's loans went up while adult loans went down by about as much? Total stays near 100, and 22% of 100 means older patrons fell from 30 loans to 22. Then the drop does show less borrowing. Prephrase: 'The rise in children's loans wasn't cancelled out by a fall in loans to other adults.'

choices.note: Tempting: it sounds like the board member's view. But the conclusion is narrower: the statistic doesn't show a decline. Negate it (older patrons' loans dipped a little) and the board member can still be right that this share figure proves nothing.
choices.negation: The number of loans to patrons over sixty-five has declined at least somewhat since the kiosks were installed.

choices.note: Tempting, because it answers the opponents' story. But the board member never argues about ease of use. The rebuttal is about the numbers. Negate it and the statistical point still stands.
choices.negation: Patrons over sixty-five find the self-checkout kiosks harder to use than younger patrons do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the children's increase was largely cancelled by fewer loans to other adults. Then total loans barely grew, the share drop reflects a real fall in older patrons' borrowing, and the rebuttal collapses.
choices.negation: The rise in loans to children has been largely offset by fewer loans to patrons who are neither children nor over sixty-five.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Even if many older patrons help with the children's program, that doesn't touch the board member's point that the total grew. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Many patrons over sixty-five take part in the library's new children's reading program.

choices.note: Irrelevant history. Ranking older patrons against other groups doesn't affect whether the share drop shows less borrowing. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Before the kiosks were installed, patrons over sixty-five did not account for a larger share of loans than every other age group did.

questions.stimulus: Labor economist: Electricians who trained through the Corvane apprenticeship program earn, on average, 20 percent more five years after finishing than electricians who learned the trade in other ways. Some argue that this gap merely reflects the program's practice of admitting only applicants with strong math scores. But the program dropped its math-score requirement fifteen years ago, and the earnings gap is just as large among those admitted since then. So the training the program provides is responsible for much of the gap.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the labor economist's argument depends?
choices: Applicants admitted since the program dropped its requirement have not, on the whole, had math scores as strong as those of applicants admitted before then.
Applicants admitted since the program dropped its requirement have, on the whole, had weaker math scores than electricians who learned the trade in other ways.
Among electricians generally, those with strong math scores do not earn more than those with weaker math scores.
No electrician who learned the trade outside the Corvane program earns more than the average graduate of the program.
The Corvane program has not changed what it teaches apprentices since it dropped its math-score requirement.
questions.explanation: Core move: a rebuttal that relies on a policy change assumes the change actually changed something. The economist answers the selection objection by noting that the gap survived the dropped requirement, but if the later apprentices still had math scores as strong as earlier ones (say, because only strong students apply), dropping the rule changed nothing and the persistence of the gap proves nothing; that's (A). The trap is (B), which differs by its comparison group: the argument needs the later apprentices' scores to have fallen relative to earlier apprentices, not to have fallen below outsiders'. (C) is tempting but too strong; the economist's point works even if math scores do affect earnings, since the gap held while the program's math advantage shrank.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The program's training is responsible for much of the 20% earnings gap.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Objection: the gap just reflects admitting strong-math applicants; reply: the math requirement was dropped fifteen years ago, and the gap is just as large among later admits.

breakdown.analysis: Dropping a rule is one thing. Did the people actually change? Maybe the program's reputation still draws only math whizzes, so the class looks the same with or without the rule. Then the gap staying put tells you nothing about training. The economist's reply only works if dropping the rule really did weaken the apprentices' math scores. Prephrase: 'Later admits weren't as strong in math as earlier admits.' This is the counterfactual-cause pattern: to credit the training, the alternative cause (selection) has to have actually been removed. Watch the comparison group in the choices.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: later admits had math scores just as strong as earlier ones. Then dropping the rule changed nothing, selection could still explain the whole gap, and the rebuttal is empty.
choices.negation: Applicants admitted since the program dropped its requirement have, on the whole, had math scores as strong as those of applicants admitted before then.

choices.note: Tempting: it's one comparison group away from the right answer. The argument needs later admits to be weaker than earlier admits, not weaker than outsiders. Negate it (later admits are still at least as strong as outsiders) and the argument survives, because their math edge still shrank while the gap held.
choices.negation: Applicants admitted since the program dropped its requirement have not, on the whole, had weaker math scores than electricians who learned the trade in other ways.

choices.note: Too strong. The economist doesn't need math to be worthless. Negate it (strong-math electricians do earn more) and the argument stands: the gap held steady even as the program stopped selecting for math.
choices.negation: Among electricians generally, those with strong math scores earn more than those with weaker math scores.

choices.note: Way too strong. The comparison is between averages. A few outsiders can out-earn the average graduate. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one electrician who learned the trade outside the Corvane program earns more than the average graduate of the program.

choices.note: Not required. If the curriculum changed, the training could still be responsible for the gap. Negation doesn't hurt the conclusion that training matters.
choices.negation: The Corvane program has changed what it teaches apprentices since it dropped its math-score requirement.

questions.stimulus: Library director: Every branch of the Ashcombe library system that hosts a weekly coding club is eligible for a technology grant this year. The Millbrook branch hosts a weekly coding club. So the Millbrook branch will be able to replace its aging public computers this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the library director's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any branch that will be able to replace its aging public computers this year is eligible for a technology grant.
The Millbrook branch's coding club is better attended than the coding club of any other branch.
Every branch that is eligible for a technology grant this year will be able to replace its aging public computers.
Technology grants awarded to Ashcombe branches may be spent only on public computers.
Some branches that do not host a coding club also have aging public computers.
questions.explanation: Core move: connect the premise's last term (eligible for a grant) to the conclusion's new term (able to replace computers). Millbrook hosts a club, so it is eligible; (C) says every eligible branch will be able to replace its computers, so the conclusion follows. The most tempting trap is (D), which ties the grants to computers, but it only restricts how grant money is spent and never guarantees that an eligible branch actually gets a grant or enough money. (A) links the same two terms in the wrong direction.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Millbrook will be able to replace its aging public computers this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Coding club → eligible for a technology grant; Millbrook hosts a coding club.

breakdown.analysis: Millbrook is eligible for a grant. So what? Eligible isn't the same as replacing computers. The argument jumps from one to the other. Chain: coding club → eligible → ??? → can replace computers. We need: eligible → can replace computers. Prephrase: 'Any branch eligible for a grant will be able to replace its computers.' New term in the conclusion with no premise behind it? That's your gap.

choices.note: Reversed. This says replacing computers → eligible. We need eligible → replacing computers.
Irrelevant. Popularity doesn't connect eligibility to new computers.
CORRECT. Coding club → eligible → can replace computers. Millbrook goes all the way through.

Tempting, because it puts grants and computers in the same sentence. But it only limits how grant money may be spent. Eligible isn't awarded, and a small grant might not cover the replacement. It doesn't guarantee anything.
Irrelevant. Other branches' computers tell us nothing about Millbrook's.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Mayfly larvae in the Sallow River survive only in stretches where the water stays below 20 degrees Celsius throughout the summer. Since the Corran Dam was completed, the stretch of the river just below the dam has no longer stayed that cool in summer. So trout will no longer be able to feed through the summer in that stretch.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the ecologist's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Trout can feed through the summer in a stretch of the Sallow only if mayfly larvae survive in that stretch.
In any stretch of the Sallow where mayfly larvae survive, trout are able to feed through the summer.
Trout in the Sallow generally prefer to feed in water that is cooler than 20 degrees Celsius.
Before the dam was completed, the stretch just below it supported more mayfly larvae than any other stretch.
Mayfly larvae are the principal food of the trout that live in the Sallow River.
questions.explanation: Core move: the conclusion introduces trout, so the assumption must tie trout feeding to the premises' mayflies as a necessary condition. The premises establish that mayfly larvae can't survive below the dam; (A) says trout can feed there only if mayflies survive, so trout can't feed there. The most tempting trap is (E): if mayflies are the trout's 'principal' food, losing them sounds fatal, but principal isn't exclusive, and trout could feed on other things. (B) gives the reversed, sufficient version of the needed link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Trout can no longer feed through the summer in the stretch below the dam.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mayfly larvae survive → water below 20°C all summer; the stretch below the dam no longer stays below 20°C.

breakdown.analysis: So no mayfly larvae below the dam. Fine. But the conclusion is about trout. Why can't trout feed without mayflies? Maybe they eat snails. Chain: not cool → no mayflies → ??? → trout can't feed. We need: no mayflies → trout can't feed, which is the same as trout feed → mayflies survive. Prephrase: 'Trout can feed in a stretch only if mayflies survive there.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Trout feed → mayflies survive. Contrapositive: no mayflies → trout can't feed. The stretch below the dam has no mayflies, so no trout feeding.
Reversed. Mayflies → trout can feed. Below the dam there are no mayflies, so this rule doesn't apply.
A preference isn't a requirement. Trout that prefer cool water can still feed in warmer water.
Irrelevant. How many mayflies the stretch used to have doesn't connect mayflies to trout.
Tempting. It sounds like losing mayflies starves the trout. But 'principal' isn't 'only'. Trout could still feed on whatever else is there. The LSAT is ultra literal: you need a must, not a mostly.

questions.stimulus: Ceramicist: A glaze that contains lead can leach it into acidic foods, so no glaze that contains lead is food-safe. Every glaze in our studio's new Heritage line reproduces a nineteenth-century recipe. Therefore, none of the Heritage glazes is food-safe.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the ceramicist's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any glaze that is not food-safe contains lead.
Most glaze recipes from the nineteenth century called for lead.
Some glazes that contain no lead are nonetheless unsafe for use with acidic foods.
Every glaze that reproduces a nineteenth-century recipe contains lead.
The studio sells the Heritage glazes mainly for decorative pieces rather than for tableware.
questions.explanation: Core move: bridge from the term in the premise about the Heritage line (nineteenth-century recipe) to the term in the rule (contains lead). With (D), every Heritage glaze reproduces an old recipe, so contains lead, so is not food-safe. The most tempting trap is (B), which points in the right direction but says only 'most', so some Heritage glazes could reproduce lead-free recipes and be food-safe. (A) reverses the lead rule: it says what's true of unsafe glazes, not what's true of leaded ones.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the Heritage glazes is food-safe.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Contains lead → not food-safe; every Heritage glaze reproduces a nineteenth-century recipe.

breakdown.analysis: Old recipe. So what? Who says old recipes contain lead? That's the missing link. Chain: Heritage → 19th-century recipe → ??? → contains lead → not food-safe. Prephrase: 'Every glaze made from a nineteenth-century recipe contains lead.' Since the conclusion says 'none', the link has to cover every Heritage glaze, so it needs 'every', not 'most'.

choices.note: Reversed. Not food-safe → lead. We need lead on the other side: old recipe → lead → not food-safe. This rule never gets us from Heritage to unsafe.
Tempting: it's the right idea. But 'most' isn't enough for 'none of the Heritage glazes'. Some Heritage glazes could copy the lead-free minority of old recipes and be perfectly food-safe.
So? Other reasons a glaze might be unsafe don't show that the Heritage glazes have any of them.
CORRECT. Heritage → 19th-century recipe → contains lead → not food-safe. Every Heritage glaze makes the trip.
Irrelevant. How the glazes are marketed doesn't change whether they are food-safe.

questions.stimulus: Town treasurer: Our charter permits money to be drawn from the reserve fund only for expenses that were unforeseeable when the year's budget was adopted. Last winter the roof of the Dell Street library collapsed under heavy snow and must now be replaced. Admittedly, nobody predicted a collapse. But an engineer's report completed months before this year's budget was adopted documented that the roof was badly deteriorated, the very condition that caused the collapse. So the replacement cannot properly be paid for from the reserve fund.
questions.stem: The treasurer's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any expense that was unforeseeable when the year's budget was adopted may properly be paid for from the reserve fund.
The members of the town council read the engineer's report before they adopted this year's budget.
An expense that nobody actually predicted can nonetheless have been foreseeable when a budget was adopted.
The roof would not have collapsed last winter if it had been repaired soon after the engineer's report was completed.
If the condition that gives rise to an expense was documented before a budget was adopted, that expense was not unforeseeable then.
