questions.explanation: Core move: the charter gives a necessary condition (reserve money → unforeseeable), so the treasurer must show the expense was not unforeseeable, and only (E) delivers that, in deliberately negative wording. The deterioration that caused the collapse was documented before the budget, so by (E) the expense was not unforeseeable, and by the charter the reserve can't pay for it. The strongest trap is (C), which answers the concession ('nobody predicted a collapse') but only says such an expense 'can' have been foreseeable, not that this one was. (B) is tempting too, but council members' reading a report makes it more likely they could foresee the cost without logically establishing that the cost was foreseeable.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The roof replacement can't properly be paid for from the reserve fund.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reserve fund → expense was unforeseeable at budget time; nobody predicted the collapse; before the budget, an engineer's report documented the deterioration that caused it.

breakdown.analysis: Documented isn't the same as foreseeable. Is it? The treasurer treats them as the same, and that's the gap. Chain: paid from reserve → unforeseeable. Contrapositive: NOT unforeseeable → can't be paid from reserve. So we need: documented cause → not unforeseeable. Full chain: cause documented before budget → expense not unforeseeable → can't use the reserve. Prephrase: 'An expense whose cause was documented before the budget wasn't unforeseeable.' Expect the right answer to sound a bit clunky; the double negative mirrors the charter's word 'unforeseeable'.

choices.note: This turns the charter around: unforeseeable → may use the reserve. It's about expenses that qualify, and we're trying to show this one doesn't. It doesn't help.

Tempting. If the council read the report, it sure seems they could have seen this coming. But 'seems' isn't proof: the report might have predicted the roof would last years. Reading a report doesn't make the expense foreseeable as a matter of logic.
Tempting, because it answers the 'Admittedly' sentence head-on. But 'can have been' only shows it's possible. We need this expense to have been foreseeable, not merely that such things can be.
Irrelevant. Whether a repair would have saved the roof tells us nothing about whether the expense was foreseeable when the budget passed.

CORRECT. The deterioration that caused the collapse was documented before the budget, so the expense was not unforeseeable. The charter allows reserve money only for unforeseeable expenses, so the replacement doesn't qualify.

questions.stimulus: Birding club president: Under our bylaws, only members who have submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons may vote in the election of club officers. Some members object that this rule shuts out the club's newest birders, and that is true. But the rule does not shut out our dues-paying members: every member who has submitted logs in each of the past three seasons has also paid this year's dues. Hence, at least some of this year's dues-paying members may vote in the election.
questions.stem: The president's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every member who has paid this year's dues has submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons.
At least one member of the club may vote in this year's election of club officers.
Any member who has submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons may vote in the election of club officers.
Some members who have submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons have paid this year's dues.
None of the club's newest birders has paid this year's dues.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'some' conclusion needs someone to exist, and the premises never say anyone can vote. The rules give vote → logs every season → paid dues, so any voter is a dues-payer; (B) supplies one voter, and that person is a dues-paying member who may vote. The trap is (C), which flips 'only members who...may' into 'any member who...may': even then, nothing says any member has actually submitted all three seasons of logs, so the group could be empty. (D) is tempting because it's already a 'some' statement, but submitting logs is only required for voting, not enough for it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least some of this year's dues-paying members may vote.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: May vote → logs in each of the past three seasons; logs in each of the past three seasons → paid this year's dues; (concession: newest birders can't vote).

breakdown.analysis: Chain: may vote → three seasons of logs → paid dues. So every voter is a payer. But does any voter exist? Nothing says so. Maybe no one met the log rule and nobody can vote at all. Then 'some payers may vote' is false. It's like 'Everyone with a ticket paid, so some payers have tickets': only if someone has a ticket. So we need: at least one member may vote. Then that member rides the chain to 'paid dues', and we have a dues-payer who may vote. The concession about newest birders is a distraction.

choices.note: Reversed. Paid dues → logs. That still doesn't get anyone to 'may vote', because logs are only required for voting, not enough for it.
CORRECT. Odd-sounding, but it fills the real gap. One voter → that voter submitted all three seasons of logs → paid dues. So at least one dues-payer may vote.

Tempting. It sounds like it unlocks the vote, and it differs from the bylaw by one word (any vs. only). But even with it, we still don't know a single member submitted three seasons of logs. If no one did, no one votes, and the conclusion fails.
Tempting, because it's already a 'some' claim. But three seasons of logs is necessary for voting, not sufficient. These log-submitting payers might still be barred for some other reason.
Irrelevant. It's about the newest birders, who can't vote anyway. It says nothing about whether any payer can vote.

questions.stimulus: This season the director of the Halden Community Choir began leading a ten-minute vocal warm-up at the start of every rehearsal. Singers reported hoarseness after rehearsals far less often this season than last season. The director concludes that the warm-up reduced hoarseness among the singers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?
choices: Several singers in the choir said that they enjoyed the warm-up.
Singers who arrived late and missed the warm-up this season reported hoarseness about as often as singers had last season.
Last season, the choir did not do any vocal warm-up before its rehearsals.
Hoarseness can be caused by colds as well as by vocal strain.
The choir added several new members at the start of this season.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a causal claim by showing the effect tracks the cause. If this season's singers who skipped the warm-up were as hoarse as everyone was last season, the drop shows up only among those who warmed up, which is what (B) says. The most tempting trap is (C): it sounds supportive, but it only restates what 'began leading a warm-up' already implies and adds no new reason to credit the warm-up. (D) and (E) raise side issues without linking the warm-up to the change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new warm-up reduced hoarseness among the singers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The warm-up began this season; reports of hoarseness after rehearsals fell sharply compared with last season.

breakdown.analysis: Hoarseness dropped after the warm-up started. But a lot can change between seasons: easier music, shorter rehearsals, a milder winter. How would we know it's the warm-up? Look at the singers who didn't get it. If they're still hoarse, the warm-up is the difference. It's like testing a new sunscreen: the best evidence is that the people who skipped it still got burned. Prephrase: those who missed the warm-up didn't improve.

choices.note: So? Enjoying the warm-up doesn't mean it reduced hoarseness.
CORRECT. Same season, same music, same rehearsals, but no warm-up, and no improvement. That isolates the warm-up as the difference.
Tempting, because it fits the director's story. But the stimulus already says the warm-up began this season. This repeats a premise; it doesn't add support.
Irrelevant on its own. Knowing hoarseness has several causes doesn't tell us whether the warm-up caused this drop. If anything, it hints at other explanations.
So? New members could make hoarseness more or less common; we can't tell. This doesn't link the warm-up to the decline.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Kesterton distribution warehouse replaced its dim overhead lights with much brighter LED fixtures. In the six months after the change, the number of orders shipped with the wrong item fell by 25 percent compared with the six months before, even though the warehouse shipped about the same number of orders. The manager concludes that the brighter lighting reduced picking errors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the manager's argument?
choices: The new LED fixtures use less electricity than the old lights did.
Picking errors at Kesterton had been declining steadily for several years before the new lights were installed.
Most of the warehouse's pickers said that they prefer working under the new lights.
Over the same period, the company's other warehouses, none of which changed their lighting, saw no decline in picking errors.
Shipping the wrong item costs the company more than any other kind of shipping error does.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen with a comparison group that rules out a general cause. If similar warehouses that kept their old lights saw no decline, a company-wide change (new software, training, products) is unlikely to explain Kesterton's drop, which points to the lighting, as (D) says. The most tempting trap is (C): workers liking the light feels like support, but a preference isn't evidence that errors fell because of the light. (B) actually weakens, since a pre-existing downward trend offers another explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lighting reduced picking errors at Kesterton.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lights were replaced; wrong-item shipments fell 25 percent over the next six months with about the same order volume.

breakdown.analysis: Errors fell after the new lights. Volume is held steady, so it isn't just fewer orders. But what about everything else the company might have changed, like new scanners, new training, a new product line? We want evidence that without the lights, errors wouldn't have fallen. It's like a student who switched desks and got better grades; you'd want to know whether everyone's grades rose that term. Prephrase: places without the new lights saw no improvement.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Saving electricity says nothing about picking errors.
This weakens. If errors were already falling for years, the drop might be the same trend continuing, with or without the lights.
Tempting, because happy workers seem to fit the story. But liking the lights doesn't show the lights reduced errors. Preference isn't performance.
CORRECT. The company's other warehouses, without new lights, saw no decline. That makes a company-wide cause unlikely and points to what was different at Kesterton: the lighting.
Irrelevant. This tells us the errors are costly, not what reduced them.

questions.stimulus: Each summer, the Tarrow County weather office estimates the county's rainfall using readings from rain gauges maintained by volunteers. This summer, the volunteers' gauges recorded, on average, 31 percent less rain than their own long-term summer averages. The office concludes that the county as a whole received substantially less rain than usual this summer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the weather office's argument?
choices: The volunteers' gauges are located in all parts of the county, including its hill district, which normally receives more rain than the lowlands.
Most of the volunteers have recorded rainfall at the same location for more than ten years.
A few of the gauges recorded more rain this summer than their long-term summer averages.
Lower-than-usual summer rainfall can significantly reduce the yields of the county's main crops.
There are more volunteer gauges in the county this summer than there were ten years ago.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a generalization by showing the sample represents the whole. The gauges speak for the county only if they cover the county; if they were clustered in one dry pocket, the hill district could have had a normal summer, so (A), which says they cover all parts, including the wetter hills, shores up the inference. The most tempting trap is (E): more gauges sounds like a better sample, but a larger sample can still be bunched in one area, and size is not coverage. (B) is the other serious contender, but long service supports the reliability of each gauge's average, not whether the gauges together represent the county.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county as a whole received substantially less rain than usual this summer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Volunteer gauges recorded, on average, 31 percent less rain than their own long-term averages.

breakdown.analysis: The gauges were dry. Was the county? That depends on where the gauges are. Volunteers put gauges where they live, maybe all in the lowland towns. Summer storms can be patchy; the hills could have been soaked while the towns stayed dry. It's like judging a whole city's traffic from cameras on one street. Prephrase: the gauges are spread across the whole county.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the gauges cover every part of the county, including the wetter hills, their combined shortfall is a fair picture of the county as a whole.
Tempting, because it makes each gauge's long-term average more trustworthy. But reliable gauges in the wrong places still miss the rest of the county. This is about accuracy, not coverage.
This is expected with any average and doesn't help. If anything it hints that some places had a wet summer.
Irrelevant. This is a consequence of low rain, not evidence that the county had low rain.
Tempting, because bigger samples sound better. But more gauges can still sit in the same few towns. Size isn't representativeness, and the comparison is each gauge against its own average anyway.

questions.stimulus: Coastal geologist: Since the town of Wexmouth built an offshore breakwater five years ago, its main beach has lost far less sand each year than it did in the decade before. Some residents attribute the change to the unusually mild storm seasons of the past five years. But storms, though less frequent, have not been absent. I conclude that the breakwater is largely responsible for the reduction in sand loss.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the geologist's argument?
choices: Several strong storms struck the Wexmouth coast during the past five years.
Most of the sand Wexmouth's beach lost before the breakwater was built was carried off during a handful of severe storms.
The breakwater cost Wexmouth considerably less to build than its engineers had projected.
Some of the residents who credit the mild storm seasons opposed building the breakwater.
Over the past five years, an unsheltered beach just up the coast, exposed to the same storms, has lost sand at about its usual rate.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen by defeating the rival explanation, not by bolstering a premise. The geologist's reply to the residents is weak, since 'storms have not been absent' doesn't show the milder seasons didn't matter; (E) supplies a beach that had the same mild storms but no breakwater and kept losing sand, so mild weather alone can't explain Wexmouth's change. The most tempting trap is (A): it echoes the geologist's own premise, but even with several strong storms, the seasons could still have been milder overall, so the residents' explanation stands. (B) actually helps the residents: if severe storms caused most past loss, fewer of them would explain the change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The breakwater is largely responsible for the reduced sand loss.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sand loss dropped after the breakwater was built; residents credit milder storms; the geologist replies that storms haven't been absent.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the geologist's rebuttal. 'Storms haven't been absent' is a weak reply. Fewer storms can still mean much less erosion. So the residents' explanation is still alive. To strengthen, we need to kill it. Best way: find a beach that had the same mild weather but no breakwater. If it kept eroding, the weather isn't the answer. It's like two neighbors with the same mild winter: only one put in storm windows, and only that one's heating bill fell. Prephrase: an unsheltered beach with the same storms didn't improve.

choices.note: Tempting, because it backs the geologist's own premise. But 'several strong storms' is compatible with seasons that were still milder than before. The residents' explanation survives, so the conclusion gains little.
This helps the residents. If severe storms caused most of the old sand loss, fewer severe storms would explain the drop without the breakwater.
Wrong dimension. What the breakwater cost has nothing to do with whether it reduced sand loss.
An attack on the residents' motives. Even if they opposed the breakwater, their explanation could be correct. This doesn't strengthen the argument.
CORRECT. Same storms, no breakwater, no improvement. That rules out mild weather as the explanation and leaves the breakwater as the difference.

questions.stimulus: Perfumer: After our house replaced the natural oakmoss extract in its fragrance Calder with a synthetic substitute, customer reports of skin irritation fell from about 1 per 2,000 bottles sold to about 1 per 9,000. A rival claims this merely reflects a change in who buys Calder, since the reformulated scent appeals to a younger clientele. But younger skin is, if anything, more prone to irritation than older skin. So the synthetic substitute is what reduced irritation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the perfumer's argument?
choices: Younger customers who experience irritation from a fragrance are less likely than older customers to report it to the fragrance's maker.
Calder's sales have risen since the reformulation, mainly because of purchases by younger customers.
Customers of different ages who experience skin irritation from a fragrance are about equally likely to report it to the fragrance's maker.
Some synthetic substitutes for natural fragrance ingredients can themselves cause skin irritation.
The synthetic substitute costs the house less per bottle than the oakmoss extract did.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the gap the rebuttal left open. The perfumer answers the rival with a claim about how often skin gets irritated, but the evidence is about how often irritation is reported; a younger clientele that reports less would cut reports without any change in irritation. (C) closes that gap by saying reporting doesn't vary with age, so the rebuttal now covers the data. The most tempting trap is (A), which is about the same issue but runs the other way: if younger customers report less, the drop in reports could come from the new clientele, which weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The synthetic substitute is what reduced skin irritation from Calder.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Reports of irritation per bottle fell from 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 9,000 after the switch; 2. A rival says the buyers changed (younger); 3. Younger skin is, if anything, more prone to irritation.

breakdown.analysis: Read the evidence word by word: it's reports of irritation, not irritation. The perfumer's rebuttal is about skin, how easily younger skin gets irritated. Fine. But what if younger customers just don't complain? They toss the bottle and move on. Then a younger clientele cuts reports even if their skin reacts more. The rebuttal never touches that. It's like a restaurant claiming its food got better because complaints fell, after its older regulars, who always wrote in, were replaced by students who never do. Prephrase: reporting rates don't differ by age.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about exactly the right issue. But it's the opposite direction. If younger customers report less, the drop in reports could be the clientele change after all. That weakens.
This supports the rival's premise that Calder's buyers got younger. It doesn't help show the substitute is the cause.

CORRECT. The data are reports, not reactions. If every age group reports irritation at the same rate, a younger clientele can't explain fewer reports, and the perfumer's point about younger skin then shows the drop isn't due to who buys Calder.
Tempting if you want to judge synthetics in general. But 'some' substitutes isn't this one, and if anything this cuts against the perfumer.
Wrong dimension. Cost has nothing to do with irritation.

questions.stimulus: In March, the perfume maker Sorrel & Vine began airing radio advertisements for its fragrance Juniper Hour for the first time. Sales of Juniper Hour in April were 30 percent higher than in February. The company's marketing director concluded that the radio advertisements were responsible for the increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director's argument?
choices: The radio advertisements cost more to produce than any advertising the company had previously done.
Some customers who bought Juniper Hour in April said that they had never heard the radio advertisements.
In March, a large chain of department stores began selling Juniper Hour, which had previously been sold only in the company's own shops.
Juniper Hour is more expensive than most of the other fragrances Sorrel & Vine sells.
Sales of Juniper Hour rose again in May, after the advertisements had been running for two months.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a causal claim by supplying another cause that changed at the same time. If Juniper Hour reached a big department store chain in the very month the ads started, that alone could explain the sales jump, as (C) says. The most tempting trap is (B): it sounds like evidence against the ads, but a few buyers who missed the ads tell us nothing about whether the ads drove the increase, since some sales happen without any advertising. (E) if anything supports the director.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The radio advertisements caused the rise in Juniper Hour sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ads began in March; April sales were 30 percent higher than February sales.

breakdown.analysis: Sales went up after the ads started. Did anything else change in March? The director assumes the ads are the only explanation. To weaken, we want a different reason sales would jump right then. It's like getting a raise the same week you start wearing a lucky tie, and crediting the tie. Prephrase: something else that happened around March boosted sales.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What the ads cost says nothing about whether they caused the sales increase.

Tempting, because it seems to show the ads didn't reach everyone. But 'some' buyers is expected: people bought Juniper Hour before any ads existed. The question is what caused the extra 30 percent, and this doesn't touch that.
CORRECT. A new, large set of stores selling the fragrance starting the same month is a strong alternative cause. The increase could come from wider availability, not the ads.
So? Price doesn't explain why sales rose between February and April, and it doesn't separate the ads from any other cause.
This leans the other way. Continued growth while the ads keep running fits the director's view, so it can't weaken it.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago the coastal town of Gullhaven banned bonfires on its beaches after dark. Since then, the number of sea turtle nests found on Gullhaven's beaches each summer has nearly doubled. Town officials conclude that the light from beach bonfires had been discouraging sea turtles from nesting there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' argument?
choices: Sea turtles are known to avoid nesting on beaches that are brightly lit at night.
Several residents of Gullhaven have been fined for lighting beach bonfires since the ban took effect.
The ban on beach bonfires was opposed by many of Gullhaven's business owners.
Gullhaven's beaches are longer than the beaches of most neighboring towns.
Over the same two years, the number of sea turtle nests also nearly doubled on nearby beaches where bonfires have always been permitted.
questions.explanation: Core move: use a comparison group to show the change would have happened anyway. If nests nearly doubled on nearby beaches that still allow bonfires, the rise at Gullhaven is likely part of a regional trend rather than an effect of the ban, which is (E). The most tempting trap is (B): it suggests the ban was not fully obeyed, but a handful of fines doesn't mean bonfires stayed common, and the ban could still have cut them sharply. (A) strengthens the officials' view.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bonfire light had been discouraging sea turtles from nesting on Gullhaven's beaches.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Bonfires were banned two years ago; nests have nearly doubled since then.

breakdown.analysis: Nests went up after the ban. But would they have gone up anyway? We have no comparison. If turtles were nesting more all along the coast, the ban gets credit it didn't earn. It's like a school crediting its new reading program when every school in the state saw the same score jump. Prephrase: show that nests rose just as much where nothing changed.

choices.note: This strengthens. If turtles avoid lit beaches, removing bonfire light should help, which is just what the officials claim.
Tempting, because it hints the ban wasn't obeyed. But a few fines don't show bonfires stayed common. The ban could still have removed most of them, so the officials' explanation survives.
Irrelevant. Business owners' opinions about the ban have nothing to do with why turtles nest.
So? Beach length was the same before and after the ban, so it can't explain the change.
CORRECT. Beaches that kept their bonfires saw the same near-doubling. That points to something affecting the whole coast, such as more turtles in the area, rather than the ban.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, about a third of the dairy farms in the Ellery Valley cooperative have switched their herds from grain-supplemented feed to a pasture-only diet. Last year, 8 percent of cows on the switched farms developed lameness, compared with 15 percent of cows on farms that kept feeding grain. The cooperative's advisor concludes that a pasture-only diet reduces a cow's risk of becoming lame.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advisor's argument?
choices: Before switching, the farms that adopted a pasture-only diet already had much lower rates of lameness than the farms that did not switch.
Cows on a pasture-only diet produce less milk, on average, than cows given grain-supplemented feed.
Lameness is more common among older cows than among younger cows.
Fewer cows in total are kept on the switched farms than on the farms that kept feeding grain.
Some of the farmers who switched to a pasture-only diet did so mainly to reduce their feed costs.
questions.explanation: Core move: show that the two groups differed before the supposed cause. If the switched farms already had much lower lameness before they changed diets, last year's gap reflects the farms, not the feed, which is (A). The most tempting trap is (C): it names a real alternative cause (age), but it never says the switched farms have younger herds, so it weakens only if you add an assumption. (D) is a numbers trap; the argument compares rates, so the total number of cows on each kind of farm doesn't matter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A pasture-only diet reduces a cow's risk of lameness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, 8 percent of cows on switched farms became lame vs. 15 percent on grain-feeding farms.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups, two rates, one difference credited to diet. But the farms chose to switch; they weren't assigned. Were they already different? If those farms always had sound-footed herds (better floors, better hoof care), the gap was there before any cow ate grass. It's like noting that students who chose an elective have higher grades and crediting the elective, when they were already the top students. Prephrase: the switched farms differed from the others in lameness before the switch.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the switched farms already had much lower lameness before changing diets, last year's 8 vs. 15 percent gap could be entirely pre-existing. The diet gets no credit.
Wrong dimension. Milk yield isn't lameness. This might matter to a farmer deciding whether to switch, but not to whether the diet lowers lameness.
Tempting, because age is a plausible alternative cause. But nothing says the switched farms have younger cows. You'd have to assume that, and you can't pick an answer on a possibility.
A numbers trap. The comparison is in percentages, so the size of each group doesn't change the rates being compared.
So? Why a farmer switched doesn't affect what the switch did to the cows' feet.

questions.stimulus: Twelve years ago, the Harlow County highway department repainted eighteen of its steel bridges, all in the same summer and by the same crew. Nine received a new zinc-rich coating; the other nine received the conventional coating the department had always used. Inspections this year found that the bridges with the new coating had, on average, less than half as much corrosion as the others. The department's engineer concludes that the new coating protects steel from corrosion far better than the conventional coating does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the engineer's argument?
choices: Some of the bridges that received the new coating showed more corrosion this year than some of the bridges that received the conventional coating.
On steel bridges, corrosion generally spreads faster during the second decade after painting than during the first.
The new coating costs considerably more to apply than the conventional coating does.
All nine bridges with the new coating are in the county's hill district, where far less road salt is used in winter.
The conventional coating has adequately protected the department's bridges for many decades.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a comparison by showing the two groups differ in something else that affects the outcome. The stimulus rules out timing and workmanship, but (D) reveals that all the new-coating bridges sit where little road salt is used, and road salt speeds corrosion, so their lower corrosion may have nothing to do with the coating. The most tempting trap is (A), because it seems to show the coating doesn't always win, but overlap between individual bridges is expected and leaves the large average difference intact. (B) is tempting too, but all eighteen bridges are the same age, so faster corrosion in the second decade affects both groups alike.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new zinc-rich coating protects steel from corrosion far better than the conventional coating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Eighteen bridges painted the same summer by the same crew; nine got each coating; this year the new-coating bridges averaged less than half the corrosion.

breakdown.analysis: The stimulus closes two doors on purpose: same year, same crew. So age and workmanship can't explain the gap. What's left? Where the bridges are. Were the two groups exposed to the same conditions? If the new coating went only on bridges that face less corrosion anyway, the comparison is rigged. It's like testing a new raincoat in Arizona and the old one in Seattle. Prephrase: the new-coating bridges face milder conditions.

choices.note: Tempting, because it seems to show the coating doesn't always win. But averages always hide some overlap. A few exceptions don't erase 'less than half as much corrosion on average.'
Tempting, because it's about how corrosion builds over time. But all eighteen bridges were painted the same summer, so they're all in their second decade together. This affects both groups equally.
Wrong dimension. Cost isn't protection. The conclusion is about which coating resists corrosion better.
CORRECT. Road salt is a major cause of corrosion, and the new-coating bridges got far less of it. Their lower corrosion could come from location, not the coating.
So? 'Adequate' isn't 'as good as the new coating.' The old coating can be adequate and still be far worse, so this doesn't touch the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Education consultant: Three years ago every high school in Marlow began a peer tutoring program in which strong math students coach struggling ones, and within two years the share of Marlow students failing ninth-grade algebra fell from 21 percent to 14 percent. Rennick's high schools resemble Marlow's in size and in their students' prior math scores. Admittedly, Rennick's teachers are, on average, less experienced than Marlow's. But the program depends on student tutors, not on teachers. So Rennick can expect a similar decline if it adopts the program.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultant's argument?
choices: Rennick's least experienced teachers are concentrated in subjects other than mathematics.
In the year that Marlow's program began, Marlow also started placing students who had failed eighth-grade math in a remedial course instead of in ninth-grade algebra.
Rennick's current failure rate in ninth-grade algebra is slightly lower than Marlow's was before its program began.
Some cities that adopted peer tutoring programs later abandoned them because of scheduling difficulties.
Many of Marlow's student tutors said that coaching others improved their own understanding of algebra.
questions.explanation: Core move: attack the evidence the analogy rests on, not the analogy itself. The consultant spends her effort on whether Rennick resembles Marlow, but (B) shows that Marlow's drop may not have come from tutoring at all: removing the students most likely to fail from ninth-grade algebra would lower the failure rate by itself, so there is no tutoring effect to transfer. The most tempting trap is (A), which engages the conceded teacher difference, but it only makes that difference matter less, which helps the consultant. (C) is tempting as a 'less room to improve' point, but a slightly lower starting rate still leaves plenty of room for a similar decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rennick can expect a decline in algebra failures similar to Marlow's if it adopts the program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Marlow's failure rate fell from 21 to 14 percent after peer tutoring began; 2. Rennick's schools are similar in size and prior scores; 3. Rennick's teachers are less experienced, but the program runs on student tutors.

breakdown.analysis: The argument has two links. Link one: tutoring caused Marlow's decline. Link two: Rennick is like Marlow. The consultant defends link two carefully, even handling an objection. Link one gets no defense at all. Did tutoring really cause the drop? If Marlow changed who takes ninth-grade algebra, the failure rate could fall without anyone learning more. It's like a gym bragging that members lost weight after it started a class, when it also stopped counting anyone over 250 pounds. Prephrase: something else explains Marlow's drop.

choices.note: Tempting, because it engages the concession about teachers. But it actually helps the consultant: if the inexperienced teachers mostly aren't in math, that difference matters even less.

CORRECT. Moving the students most likely to fail out of ninth-grade algebra would lower its failure rate on its own. So Marlow's decline may not be a tutoring effect, and there's nothing for Rennick to copy.
Tempting as a 'less room to improve' point. But 'slightly lower' still leaves room for a similar drop, so it barely touches the prediction.
So? Other cities' scheduling problems say nothing about whether the program lowers failure rates, or whether Rennick would keep it.
Irrelevant. Gains for the tutors don't bear on whether struggling students passed algebra, or on whether Rennick would see the same result.

questions.stimulus: Last year the number of passengers flying out of Dunmore Regional Airport rose by nearly 15 percent. Over the same period, however, the number of flights departing from the airport fell by about a tenth.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Several other airports within a two-hour drive of Dunmore also reported increases in passenger numbers last year.
The average price of a ticket on flights departing from Dunmore rose slightly last year.
Last year the airlines serving Dunmore replaced many of their small aircraft with planes that carry substantially more passengers.
Last year two of the airlines that had offered flights from Dunmore ended their service at the airport.
Most of the passengers who flew out of Dunmore last year were traveling for business rather than for leisure.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the one fact that lets both halves be true at once. More passengers on fewer flights is no puzzle if each flight carries more people, and C says the airlines switched to much larger planes. The most tempting trap is D, because it explains why there were fewer flights; but it does nothing to explain how passenger numbers rose anyway, so it resolves only half the puzzle. A is about other airports, and B, if anything, makes the passenger increase harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Passengers flying out of Dunmore rose almost 15 percent, but departing flights fell about 10 percent.

breakdown.analysis: How can more people fly on fewer flights? Easy: each flight has to carry more people. That means bigger planes or fuller planes. We need an answer that says the average flight held more passengers. It's like a bus company that runs fewer buses but switches to double-deckers: fewer trips, more riders.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other airports growing tells us nothing about how Dunmore fit more passengers onto fewer flights.
So? Higher prices would, if anything, push passenger numbers down. That makes the rise harder to explain, not easier.
CORRECT. Bigger planes mean more seats per flight. Fewer flights times more seats per flight can easily equal more passengers. Both facts now fit.

Tempting. This explains the drop in flights. But the puzzle has two halves, and this leaves the other one standing: losing two airlines should cut passengers, not raise them. A half-explanation isn't a resolution.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Why people travel doesn't tell us how more of them fit on fewer flights.

questions.stimulus: At the Fenwick Wildlife Rehabilitation Center, injured owls that receive daily physical therapy are less likely to be successfully released back into the wild than are injured owls that receive no therapy at all. Nevertheless, the center’s veterinarians are confident that the therapy improves an injured owl’s chances of being released.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Owls that are successfully released from the center are rarely brought back to it with new injuries.
Daily handling during therapy can make some owls less wary of people, a trait that endangers them after release.
The center treats more injured owls each year than does any other rehabilitation facility in the region.
Veterinarians at most other wildlife rehabilitation centers also recommend physical therapy for injured owls.
The center gives daily therapy only to owls whose wing injuries are too severe to heal properly without it.
questions.explanation: Core move: notice that the two groups being compared may not start out alike. If therapy goes only to the owls with the worst injuries (E), those owls would be released less often even if therapy helps each of them, so the vets' confidence and the lower release rate are compatible. The most tempting trap is B, because it explains why therapy owls are released less often; but it does so by saying therapy hurts, which makes the veterinarians' confidence harder to understand rather than easier. D just adds more people who share the vets' view, and A and C don't touch the comparison.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Owls that get daily therapy are released less often than owls that get none, yet the vets are confident the therapy improves an owl's chances of release.

breakdown.analysis: If therapy helps, why do therapy owls do worse? Ask who gets therapy. If the center gives therapy to the most badly hurt owls, those owls start out far behind. Therapy could lift them a lot and they'd still trail the owls with minor injuries. We need an answer that says the therapy group started out worse off. It's like noticing that hospital patients who get surgery die more often than patients who get a bandage. The surgery isn't the problem; the surgery patients were sicker.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What happens after a successful release doesn't explain why therapy owls are released less often in the first place.

Tempting. This does explain why therapy owls are released less often. But it explains it by saying the therapy hurts them. Then why are the vets confident it helps? This answer resolves one side by making the other side worse.
So? The center's size tells us nothing about the difference between the two groups of owls.
This just says more vets agree. Agreement isn't an explanation. The puzzle is how the vets can be right given the release numbers, and this doesn't touch that.

CORRECT. The therapy owls are the worst-injured owls. They'd be released less often no matter what, so the lower release rate doesn't show the therapy fails. The vets can be right that it improves each owl's chances.

questions.stimulus: Ferry operator: Our two routes across Mell Sound are the same length, and the boats on the eastern route are newer and faster than those on the western route. Nevertheless, over the past year, eastern-route crossings arrived behind schedule much more often than western-route crossings did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The timetable for the eastern route allows considerably less time for each crossing than the timetable for the western route does.
Storms disrupted crossings on Mell Sound more often during the past year than in any previous year.
The eastern route carries far more passengers in the summer months than in the winter months.
The older boats on the western route were taken out of service for repairs more often than the eastern route’s boats were.
Passengers on the eastern route complained about late arrivals more often than did passengers on the western route.
questions.explanation: Core move: see that 'behind schedule' is measured against each route's own schedule, not against the clock. If the eastern timetable gives each crossing much less time (A), faster boats can still miss it more often. The most tempting trap is B: bad weather does cause late arrivals, but the storms hit the whole sound, so they don't explain why one route ran late more than the other. D makes the western route look worse, deepening the puzzle, and E merely restates that the eastern route was late more often.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The eastern route has newer, faster boats on an equally long crossing, but its crossings arrived behind schedule more often than the western route's.

breakdown.analysis: Faster boats, same distance, more often late. Late compared to what? Compared to the schedule. Being 'behind schedule' depends on the boat's speed AND on how much time the timetable allows. Watch that relative word. We need an answer that says the eastern schedule is tighter. It's like a fast runner who misses a 10-minute target more often than a slow runner misses a 20-minute target.

choices.note: CORRECT. The eastern timetable is tighter. Fast boats facing a much tighter schedule can run late more often than slow boats on a generous one. Both facts fit.

Tempting. Storms really do make ferries late, so this feels like an explanation. But the storms hit Mell Sound, which both routes cross. A cause that affects both routes can't explain a difference between them. In a comparison paradox, you need something that differs between the groups.
Wrong comparison. This compares the eastern route with itself across seasons. The puzzle is eastern versus western.
Opposite. If the western route's boats were out for repairs more often, the western route should have had more trouble, not less. This deepens the puzzle.
This restates the puzzle. More complaints about lateness is just another sign that the eastern route ran late more. It doesn't say why.

questions.stimulus: To reduce the time its attorneys spend on initial interviews, the Hartsfield legal aid clinic began requiring every applicant to complete a detailed online intake form before being given an appointment. Since then, the average length of an initial interview at the clinic has increased, yet the total amount of attorney time spent on initial interviews has decreased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Attorneys now use the information on the intake form to ask applicants more detailed follow-up questions during initial interviews.
Since the requirement took effect, the number of people applying to the clinic for help has increased.
Many applicants find the online intake form difficult to complete and ask the clinic’s nonattorney staff for help with it.
The intake form lets the clinic identify, before any interview, applicants whose problems the clinic does not handle, and interviews with such applicants had typically been brief.
Before the requirement took effect, many interviews were lengthy discussions with applicants who turned out to have problems the clinic does not handle.
questions.explanation: Core move: separate an average from a total. If the form screens out applicants the clinic can't help, there are fewer interviews, so total time falls; and because those screened-out interviews had been short (D), dropping them raises the average length of the ones that remain. The strongest trap is E, which also screens out ineligible applicants, but it says those interviews were lengthy; removing long interviews would lower the average, so E explains the falling total but not the rising average. A explains the rising average but not the falling total, and B makes the falling total harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: After the intake form was required, the average initial interview got longer, but the total attorney time spent on initial interviews went down.

breakdown.analysis: How can each interview get longer while the total shrinks? Total = number of interviews × average length. So there must be fewer interviews. And if the interviews that disappeared were the short ones, the average of the ones left goes UP. We need an answer that cuts out short interviews. Imagine a class where two students scoring 40 drop out: the class average rises even though no one's score changed, and the total points fall.

choices.note: Tempting. This explains why the average interview is longer. But by itself it should make the total go up too. Half a resolution isn't a resolution: nothing here explains the falling total.
Opposite. More applicants means more interviews, which, with longer interviews, should push the total up. This deepens the puzzle.
Irrelevant. Help with the form comes from nonattorney staff. The puzzle is about attorney time in interviews.

CORRECT. The form weeds out people the clinic can't help before they're interviewed, so there are fewer interviews and the total falls. Those weeded-out interviews had been short, so removing them raises the average length of the interviews that remain. Both facts explained.

Tempting, and very close to the right answer. It also screens out ineligible applicants, which explains the falling total. But it says their interviews were lengthy. Cut out long interviews and the average gets SHORTER. One word ('lengthy' vs. 'brief') flips the result.

questions.stimulus: Kite maker: Kites made with our new lightweight fabric can stay aloft in lighter winds than can kites made with our older, heavier fabric. Yet at last month’s Carrow Kite Festival, where winds were light all day, more of our older-fabric kites than our new-fabric kites stayed aloft for the full hour of the endurance competition.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Many more older-fabric kites than new-fabric kites were entered in the festival’s endurance competition.
In strong winds, kites made with the older fabric generally stay aloft longer than kites made with the new fabric.
The new fabric frays quickly where it rubs against a kite’s frame, so new-fabric kites often tear during flights lasting longer than half an hour.
Most of the new-fabric kites in the endurance competition were flown by people who had never before competed at a kite festival.
Most fliers of new-fabric kites at the festival used the heavy flying lines made for older kites, which cancel the new fabric’s advantage in light winds.
questions.explanation: Core move: in an EXCEPT question, confirm that four choices resolve the puzzle and find the one that only sounds as if it does. B is about strong winds, but the festival's winds were light all day, so the older fabric's strong-wind advantage cannot explain these results. The most tempting trap is A, which looks irrelevant and so gets picked as the EXCEPT; but the stimulus says 'more of' the older kites stayed up, an absolute count, and if far more older kites were entered, more of them could stay aloft even if a larger share of the new kites did. C, D, and E each give a reason the new-fabric kites failed at this festival despite their light-wind advantage.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: New-fabric kites fly in lighter winds than older-fabric kites, yet at a light-wind festival more older-fabric kites than new-fabric kites stayed up for the full hour.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers explain the result and the right answer doesn't. Read the stimulus exactly. It says 'more of' the older kites stayed up. That's a count, not a percentage. And it says winds were light 'all day.' So anything about strong winds is off the table. Watch both details: a count can be explained by numbers entered, and a light-wind puzzle can't be explained by strong-wind facts.

choices.note: This helps, so it's wrong here. Tempting to pick as the EXCEPT because it seems beside the point. But 'more of' is a count. If 40 old kites and 5 new ones were entered, 20 old kites could stay up while all 5 new ones did too. More older kites staying aloft is then no surprise.

CORRECT. This is the one that doesn't help. It's about strong winds, and the festival had light winds all day. The older fabric's advantage in strong winds can't explain what happened in light winds. It sounds like an explanation because it gives the older fabric an edge, but it's the wrong conditions.

This helps, so it's wrong here. The endurance competition lasts a full hour, and new-fabric kites tend to tear on flights longer than half an hour. That's a reason new kites came down even though the light winds suited them.
This helps, so it's wrong here. If most new-fabric kites were in the hands of first-timers, flier inexperience could explain why fewer of them stayed up, whatever the fabric's advantage.
This helps, so it's wrong here. The heavy lines cancel the new fabric's light-wind advantage, so at this festival the new kites didn't actually have their usual edge.

questions.stimulus: Two months ago, Orwin Dairy covered the concrete floor of the pen where its cows wait to be milked with soft rubber mats. Since then, the average time it takes to move the herd through the milking parlor has dropped by nearly a fifth. The farm manager concludes that the mats, by making the cows more comfortable while they wait, have made them move more willingly into the parlor.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the farm manager's argument?
choices: How much did the rubber mats cost to purchase and install?
Do the cows produce more milk now than they did before the mats were installed?
Are rubber mats also used in the waiting pens of other dairies in the region?
Do the farm's workers prefer standing on the mats to standing on concrete?
Did the dairy make any other change to its milking routine at about the time the mats were installed?
questions.explanation: Core move: an evaluate question about a causal claim asks you to check for another cause. If the dairy also changed its milking routine (new staff, new schedule, new gates) when the mats went in, that change could explain the faster milking; if nothing else changed, the mats look more likely to be the cause, so (E) matters either way. The most tempting trap is (B): more milk sounds like a sign of comfortable cows, but the conclusion is about moving into the parlor, and either answer leaves that unaffected.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mats made the cows more comfortable and so more willing to move into the parlor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mats went in two months ago; time to move the herd through the parlor dropped by nearly a fifth.

breakdown.analysis: Faster milking after the mats. Was it the mats? Maybe the dairy also hired a better hand, changed the schedule, or fixed a sticky gate. A good evaluate answer has two answers that push opposite ways: 'yes, other changes' weakens; 'no, nothing else changed' strengthens. It's like crediting new running shoes for a faster mile; you'd want to know if you also started training. Prephrase: did anything else change at the same time?

choices.note: Irrelevant. Cost tells you whether the mats were worth buying, not whether they caused faster milking.
Tempting, because more milk seems like a sign of happier cows. But the conclusion is about moving into the parlor. Milk yield could go either way without telling us why the cows move faster.
So? What other dairies use doesn't tell us what caused the change at Orwin.
Wrong group. The argument is about the cows' comfort, not the workers'.
CORRECT. If something else changed at the same time, it could explain the faster milking. If nothing did, the mats become the likely cause. Either answer moves the argument.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Drummond Regional Weather Service stopped describing the chance of rain as a percentage and began using phrases such as 'rain likely' and 'a slight chance of showers.' Since then, the number of calls the service receives from people asking what its forecasts mean has fallen by 40 percent. The service's director concludes that the new phrasing is easier for the public to understand than percentages were.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the director's argument?
choices: whether the number of people who consult the service's forecasts has changed significantly since last year
whether the service's forecasts have been more accurate this year than they were last year
whether the service consulted members of the public before adopting the new phrasing
whether the service's forecasters find the new phrases easier to write than percentages
whether other regional weather services still describe the chance of rain as a percentage
questions.explanation: Core move: a count can fall because the pool shrank, not because the rate changed. Fewer confused callers supports the director only if roughly as many people still use the forecasts; if far fewer people consult them now, fewer calls would follow regardless of the phrasing, so (A) is what we need to know. The most tempting trap is (B): accuracy is about forecasts and sounds important, but the conclusion is about how understandable the phrasing is, not whether the predictions come true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new phrasing is easier for the public to understand than percentages were.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the switch to phrases, calls asking what forecasts mean fell 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer confused calls. Does that mean less confusion? Only if the same number of people are reading the forecasts. If half the audience moved to a phone app, calls drop with no change in understanding. It's like a store saying its new signs are clearer because fewer customers asked for directions, during a month when foot traffic fell by half. Prephrase: did the number of forecast users change?

choices.note: CORRECT. If far fewer people use the forecasts now, fewer calls would follow regardless of the phrasing. If the audience is the same size, the drop in calls is better evidence of clearer wording.
Tempting, because accuracy sounds central to forecasting. But the LSAT is specific: the conclusion is about understanding the wording, not about whether the predictions are right.
So? Asking the public first doesn't tell us whether the phrasing actually turned out easier to understand.
Wrong group. The argument is about the public's understanding, not the forecasters' convenience.
Irrelevant. What other services do says nothing about whether Drummond's change helped its own public.

questions.stimulus: Six months ago, the Brisco warehouse began paying its pickers a bonus for every order they fill beyond a daily quota. Since then, the number of orders filled per picker-hour has risen by 12 percent. The warehouse manager concludes that the bonus has made the pickers more productive.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the manager's argument?
choices: Has the warehouse hired additional pickers since the bonus was introduced?
Do most of the pickers regard the bonus as a fair reward for their extra effort?
Is the bonus paid to the pickers weekly or monthly?
Has the average number of items in each order changed since the bonus was introduced?
Have the warehouse's total shipping costs risen over the past six months?
questions.explanation: Core move: test whether the measure really tracks the thing concluded. 'Orders per picker-hour' counts orders, but an order can be one item or thirty; if orders got smaller, pickers could fill more of them with no extra effort, so (D) bears directly on whether the 12 percent rise reflects productivity. The most tempting trap is (A): more pickers sounds like it could inflate output, but the measure is already per picker-hour, so staffing levels are built into it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bonus made the pickers more productive.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the bonus began, orders filled per picker-hour rose 12 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Orders per hour went up. Is an order a fixed amount of work? No. If customers are now ordering two items instead of five, a picker fills more orders per hour while doing the same work or less. It's like a cashier bragging about serving more customers per hour in a week when everyone bought a single coffee. Prephrase: did the size of a typical order change?

choices.note: Tempting, because more staff usually means more output. But the measure is per picker-hour, so it already adjusts for how many pickers there are. Hiring doesn't change the comparison.
So? Whether pickers think the bonus is fair doesn't show whether their output really rose.
Irrelevant. How often the bonus is paid doesn't tell us whether productivity actually increased.
CORRECT. If orders got smaller, the 12 percent rise could happen with no gain in productivity. If order size held steady, the rise reflects real extra work. Either answer matters.
Too far removed. Total shipping costs depend on many things, like fuel, carriers and volume, and say nothing clear about pickers' productivity.

questions.stimulus: Choir director: Since we moved the Vellmar Youth Choir's rehearsals from Saturday mornings to Thursday evenings last spring, membership has grown by a third. Some parents credit the new music program at Vellmar's middle school for the growth. But that program did not begin until this fall, months after our membership started to climb. So the growth must be due to the rehearsal change.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the choir director's argument?
choices: whether the middle school's music program has been praised by music educators in the region
how much of the choir's increase in membership has occurred since the middle school's music program began
whether the parents who credit the music program have children enrolled in it
whether other youth choirs in the region rehearse on weekday evenings
whether the Saturday morning rehearsals lasted longer than the Thursday evening rehearsals do
questions.explanation: Core move: spot the gap in a timing rebuttal. The director shows the growth started before the school program, but the conclusion credits the rehearsal change with all of the growth; if most of the new members joined this fall, the program could account for much of it. So (B), how much of the growth came after the program began, decides whether the rebuttal works. The most tempting trap is (A), because it is about the rival explanation, but the program's reputation says nothing about when or whether its students joined the choir.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The choir's growth is due to the rehearsal change.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rehearsals moved last spring; membership is up a third; the school program parents credit began only this fall, after membership started to climb.

breakdown.analysis: The director's reply is about when the growth started. But the conclusion is about all of the growth. 'Started to climb' before fall doesn't mean most of the climb happened before fall. Imagine 3 new members in spring and summer, then 20 in September. The climb started early, but the school program could explain most of it. It's like a coach crediting a new drill for a winning season because the first win came before the star player arrived. Prephrase: how much of the growth came after the program started?

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the rival explanation. But a program's reputation tells us nothing about whether its students joined the choir, or when.
CORRECT. If most of the growth came after the program began, the director's timing point collapses and the program may explain much of it. If almost all came before, the director's rebuttal holds.
An attack on the parents' motives. Even biased parents can be right. Their reasons for saying it don't tell us what caused the growth.
So? What other choirs do says nothing about why Vellmar's membership grew.
Irrelevant on its own. Rehearsal length doesn't tell us whether the schedule change, rather than the school program, caused the growth.

questions.stimulus: City engineer: Two years ago we widened the Corran Street bridge, adding a separate lane for cyclists. Since then, collisions between cyclists and pedestrians on that bridge have fallen by 30 percent, while on the nearby Mill Street bridge, which was not widened, such collisions have risen by 10 percent. Critics point out that new lighting was installed on the Corran Street bridge at the same time. But the Mill Street bridge received identical lighting that same month. So the widening, not the lighting, is what reduced collisions on the Corran Street bridge.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the engineer's argument?
choices: Was the new lighting on the two bridges installed mainly to reduce collisions or mainly to deter crime?
Has the combined number of cyclists and pedestrians crossing the two bridges changed over the past two years?
Has the share of the two bridges' combined cyclist and pedestrian traffic that uses the Corran Street bridge changed over the past two years?
Are collisions between cyclists and pedestrians more likely to cause serious injuries than other collisions on the bridges?
Did the critics who cited the new lighting oppose the widening project before it began?
questions.explanation: Core move: the figures are counts, so check whether traffic moved between the two bridges. If many people switched from Corran Street to Mill Street, Corran Street's collisions would fall and Mill Street's would rise even if the widening did nothing; if each bridge kept its share, the comparison stands, so (C) matters either way. The most tempting trap is (B), which differs by one idea: a change in the two bridges' combined traffic would affect both bridges together and can't explain why they moved in opposite directions. (A) tempts because the lighting was the critics' point, but the engineer's rebuttal depends on what the lighting was, not why it was installed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The widening, not the new lighting, reduced cyclist-pedestrian collisions on the Corran Street bridge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Collisions fell 30 percent on Corran Street and rose 10 percent on the unwidened Mill Street bridge; 2. Critics cite new lighting; 3. Mill Street got identical lighting the same month.

breakdown.analysis: The lighting rebuttal is solid; both bridges got it. So look elsewhere. Are those numbers rates or counts? Counts. Fewer collisions can just mean fewer people. And look at the pattern: Corran down, Mill up. That's exactly what you'd see if traffic shifted from one bridge to the other, say during two years of construction detours, and never came back. It's like a store claiming its new layout cut shoplifting, when half its customers started shopping at the store next door. Prephrase: did traffic shift between the bridges?

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the critics' point. But the engineer's rebuttal works because the lighting was identical on both bridges. Why it was installed doesn't change what it did.

Tempting, and nearly the right answer. But combined traffic hits both bridges together. It can't explain why one bridge's collisions fell while the other's rose. What matters is how the traffic is split.

CORRECT. If traffic shifted from Corran Street to Mill Street, that alone would produce fewer collisions on one and more on the other, with no help from the widening. If the split held steady, the widening looks like the cause.
Wrong dimension. How serious the collisions are doesn't bear on what reduced their number.
An attack on the critics' motives. Their point about lighting is answered on the merits already, and their history doesn't affect what caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: Every project funded from Dunmore's capital budget must be reviewed by the city's planning commission. The planning commission does not review any project that lacks a completed environmental assessment. The proposed Ash Street footbridge is funded from the capital budget.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The planning commission has approved the proposed Ash Street footbridge.
Every project that has a completed environmental assessment is reviewed by the planning commission.
Any project that the planning commission reviews is funded from the capital budget.
The Ash Street footbridge is the only capital project with a completed environmental assessment.
The proposed Ash Street footbridge has a completed environmental assessment.
questions.explanation: Core move: chain two necessary conditions forward. Capital funding requires a commission review, and a review requires a completed environmental assessment, so the footbridge must have one, which is (E). The tempting trap is (A), which swaps 'reviewed' for 'approved'; a review can end in rejection. (B) and (C) each reverse one of the rules.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Capital budget → reviewed by the commission; 2. Reviewed → completed environmental assessment; 3. The footbridge is funded from the capital budget.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: capital budget → reviewed → assessment done. The footbridge is in the capital budget, so it rides the chain all the way. Prephrase: the footbridge is reviewed and has a completed assessment. Watch for word swaps: reviewed isn't approved.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'reviewed' feels like 'approved'. It isn't. The commission might review the footbridge and reject it. The LSAT is ultra specific about words.
Reverses rule 2. An assessment is required for review, not a ticket to one.
Reverses rule 1. Capital projects get reviewed, but the commission might review other projects too.
We don't know this. Nothing says the footbridge is the only one. 'Only' claims are rarely supported.
CORRECT. Capital budget → reviewed → completed assessment. The footbridge has one.

questions.stimulus: Most members of the Fenmoor Birding Club own a spotting scope. Every member who owns a spotting scope takes part in the club's winter shorebird count. The winter shorebird count is held only on days when the tide is low in the early morning.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Every member who takes part in the winter shorebird count owns a spotting scope.
Members of the club who do not own a spotting scope do not take part in the winter count.
Most club members take part in an activity held only when the tide is low in the early morning.
The club schedules most of its activities for days when the tide is low in the early morning.
Spotting scopes are more useful for counting shorebirds than for any other kind of birdwatching.
questions.explanation: Core move: carry a 'most' through an 'every' rule. Most members own a scope, every scope owner joins the winter count, and the count is held only at early low tide, so most members take part in an early-low-tide activity, which is (C). The tempting trap is (B), which negates the rule: owning a scope guarantees taking part, but members without scopes might join the count too. (D) stretches one activity into most of the club's activities.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most members own a scope; 2. Scope → takes part in the winter count; 3. Winter count → held only at early-morning low tide.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the majority: most members → scope → winter count. So most members do the winter count. And the winter count happens only at early low tide. So most members do something held only at early low tide. That's a 'most' carried through 'every' rules, which always works. Watch for the trap that negates the rule: no scope doesn't mean no count.

choices.note: Reverses rule 2. Scope owners all count shorebirds, but counters might include people who borrow a scope or just use binoculars.
Tempting. It feels like the flip side of rule 2. But it's a negation error: scope → count doesn't mean no scope → no count. Anyone can join the count.
CORRECT. Most members → scope → winter count, and the count is held only at early low tide. So most members take part in an early-low-tide activity.
We only know about one activity. 'Most of its activities' stretches a single event into a scheduling habit.
Unsupported comparison. The stimulus never compares uses of spotting scopes.

questions.stimulus: At Quarrystone Pottery, each apprentice is assigned either to the wheel room or to the kiln yard, but never to both. Every apprentice assigned to the kiln yard has completed the studio's fire-safety course. No apprentice assigned to the wheel room teaches the Saturday beginners' class.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: One of the apprentices who teaches the Saturday beginners' class has not completed the fire-safety course.
Some apprentice who has completed the fire-safety course is assigned to the wheel room.
None of the apprentices assigned to the kiln yard teaches the Saturday beginners' class.
Some apprentices who have not completed the fire-safety course do not teach any class.
Every apprentice who has completed the fire-safety course teaches the Saturday beginners' class.
questions.explanation: Core move: use an either/or rule to turn 'not one' into 'the other', then chain. An apprentice who teaches the Saturday class can't be in the wheel room, so must be in the kiln yard, so must have completed the fire-safety course; (A) contradicts that. The tempting trap is (C), which sounds like it breaks the rules, but nothing requires any kiln-yard apprentice to teach; maybe no apprentice teaches the class at all. (E) feels too sweeping, but it's possible: the facts never stop a fire-safety graduate from teaching.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Each apprentice: wheel room OR kiln yard, not both; 2. Kiln yard → completed fire safety; 3. Wheel room → doesn't teach Saturday.

breakdown.analysis: Find the chain. Contrapositive of 3: teaches Saturday → not wheel room. Rule 1: not wheel → kiln yard. Rule 2: kiln yard → fire safety. So: apprentice teaches Saturday → kiln yard → fire safety. An apprentice who teaches Saturday without fire safety is impossible. Everything else is loose. For a CANNOT question, the four wrong answers are just things that could happen.

choices.note: CORRECT. Saturday teacher → not wheel → kiln yard → fire safety. An apprentice teacher without fire safety breaks the chain.
Could be true. Kiln-yard apprentices must have the course, but nothing stops a wheel-room apprentice from taking it too.
Tempting, because it feels like someone has to teach. But nothing says any apprentice teaches the Saturday class. A staff potter might teach it. This can be true.
Could be true. Wheel-room apprentices may lack the course, and they don't teach Saturday. Easy to picture.

Sounds extreme, but it's allowed. Picture a studio where only the kiln-yard apprentices have taken the course and all of them teach on Saturday. No rule is broken. (It would fail only if some wheel-room apprentice had the course, and nothing says one does.)

questions.stimulus: Users of the Stride fitness app who switched on its optional daily reminder logged workouts on twice as many days, on average, as users who did not. Yet when Stride's developers randomly selected half of the app's users to receive the daily reminder automatically, those users logged workouts on no more days, on average, than the users who were not selected.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The daily reminder does not increase the number of days on which any Stride user logs a workout.
Users who choose to switch on the daily reminder differ in some respect other than receiving the reminder from users who do not.
Most users who switched on the daily reminder would have logged workouts on just as many days without it.
Users who switch on the daily reminder exercise more often than users who do not switch it on.
Sending reminders to users automatically is less effective than letting users decide whether to receive them.
questions.explanation: Core move: when a self-selected comparison shows a big gap and a random assignment shows none, the self-selected groups must differ in some other way. Whether the choosers were simply more motivated or the reminder works only for people who want it, choosers differ from non-choosers in something besides getting the reminder, so (B) is supported either way. The strongest trap is (C): it is the natural conclusion if choosers are just more motivated, but the facts also fit a reminder that helps only users who chose it, in which case most choosers would log fewer days without it. (A) is too strong for the same reason, and (D) swaps logging workouts for actually exercising.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Users who switched the reminder on logged workouts on twice as many days as users who didn't; 2. Users randomly given the reminder logged no more days than users not given it.

breakdown.analysis: Fact 1 looks like the reminder works. Fact 2 says it doesn't, at least when handed out at random. How can both be true? The people who switch it on must be different. Maybe they're keener. Or maybe the reminder only works on people who ask for it. Either way, choosers differ from non-choosers in some way besides getting the reminder. That's the safe inference. Watch for answers that pick one of those two stories as fact; both are still possible. It's like noticing that people who buy gym memberships are fitter: the people who sign up aren't a random slice of the population.

choices.note: Too strong. 'Any user'? The random trial shows no average effect. The reminder could still help some users, maybe exactly the ones who choose it.

CORRECT. If choosers were just like everyone else, switching on the reminder would act like being randomly given it: no effect. The big gap means choosers differ in some other way, whether in motivation or in how they respond to reminders.

Tempting. It's the 'they're just more motivated' story, and that may be right. But the facts also fit a reminder that works only for people who want it. Then choosers would log fewer days without it. The stimulus can't tell these apart.
Logging isn't exercising. The facts are about logged workouts. Choosers might simply be better at recording what they do.

Unsupported. We know automatic reminders had no average effect, but we don't know that letting users choose has any effect either. The choosers' higher numbers might have nothing to do with the reminder.

questions.stimulus: Every resident physician at Calder General who rotated through the intensive care unit this year also rotated through the emergency department. Most of the residents who rotated through the emergency department this year were first-year residents. No first-year resident rotated through the intensive care unit this year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Some of the residents who rotated through the emergency department this year were not first-year residents.
Most of Calder General's first-year residents rotated through the emergency department this year.
At least one resident who rotated through the intensive care unit this year was not a first-year resident.
Fewer than half of the residents who rotated through the emergency department this year also rotated through the intensive care unit.
Every resident who rotated through the emergency department this year but was not a first-year resident also rotated through the intensive care unit.
