questions.explanation: Core move: combine 'most' with an exclusion to bound a subgroup. Every ICU resident was in the ED, and none was a first-year, so ICU residents sit entirely in the non-first-year part of the ED group, which is less than half of it; that's (D). The sharpest traps are (A) and (C), which feel like they follow but each assumes someone exists: 'most' can mean all, so every ED resident might have been a first-year, and then no one rotated through the ICU at all. (B) reverses the direction of 'most'.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. ICU → ED; 2. Most ED residents were first-years; 3. First-year → not ICU.

breakdown.analysis: Picture the ED group as 10 residents. At least 6 are first-years (fact 2). First-years can't be in the ICU (fact 3), and everyone in the ICU came from the ED group (fact 1). So the ICU residents are drawn only from the at most 4 non-first-years. Under half. That's the inference, and it holds even if the ICU group is empty. Now the subset trap: 'most' on the LSAT means more than half, possibly all. So the ED group might be 100% first-years, the ICU empty, and any 'some resident was...' claim false. Be suspicious of answers that need someone to exist.

choices.note: Tempting: 'most were first-years' sounds like 'some weren't'. But 'most' includes 'all'. If every ED resident was a first-year, this is false.
Reverses the 'most'. We know most ED residents were first-years, not that most first-years were in the ED. There could be dozens of first-years who never went near it.
Tempting: ICU residents can't be first-years, so surely one wasn't. But that only works if someone rotated through the ICU. Nothing says anyone did.
CORRECT. ICU residents are all ED residents who aren't first-years, and non-first-years are under half of the ED group. So ICU residents are under half of it too, even if there are none.
Unsupported. Non-first-years in the ED are the only ones who could be in the ICU, but nothing says they all were.

questions.stimulus: Someone who finds an injured wild animal should take it to a licensed wildlife rehabilitation center rather than try to care for it at home, unless no such center can be reached within a day.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Marta cared for an injured heron at home for a week; since the heron recovered fully, she acted properly.
Jun drove a fledgling sparrow to a licensed center four hours away; he should instead have cared for it at home, where it would have been less frightened.
Priya should have taken the injured fox she found to a licensed center, even though the nearest one was a two-day drive away.
Tomas should not have kept the injured owl he found at home, since a licensed rehabilitation center was only an hour’s drive away.
Lena, a licensed rehabilitator, should release the hawk she has been treating as soon as it is able to fly.
questions.explanation: Core move: match the facts to the principle's rule and its exception. The rule says take the animal to a licensed center unless none can be reached within a day; Tomas's center was an hour away, so the exception doesn't apply and keeping the owl at home was wrong (D). The most tempting trap is A, because the heron's recovery makes Marta's choice feel justified; but the principle doesn't care how things turn out, and nothing says she couldn't reach a center. C gets the exception backward, since a two-day drive is exactly when home care is allowed.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Find an injured wild animal → take it to a licensed center, not home care. Exception: no center can be reached within a day.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right judgment must involve a center reachable within a day and say the animal belongs at the center (or a center out of reach and allow home care).

breakdown.analysis: Two parts: the rule (go to a licensed center) and the exception (no center within a day). The right answer has to line up with both. So what if things worked out? The principle is about what you should do, not how lucky you got. Look for someone near a center who kept the animal at home anyway, and a judgment that says that was wrong.

choices.note: Tempting. The heron recovered, so it feels like Marta did fine. But the principle doesn't judge by results. And we aren't told she couldn't reach a center, so the exception isn't triggered. Under the principle, she should have taken the heron to a center.
Opposite. Jun did exactly what the principle says: a center four hours away is reachable within a day. Calling that a mistake contradicts the principle.
This reverses the exception. A two-day drive means no center can be reached within a day, which is exactly when home care is allowed. The principle doesn't require the trip here.
CORRECT. The center was an hour away, well within a day, so the exception doesn't apply. The principle says the owl belonged at the center, so keeping it at home was wrong.
Irrelevant. The principle is about what someone who finds an injured animal should do, not when a licensed rehabilitator should release one.

questions.stimulus: Chess club president: Our club should not move its weekly tournament from Tuesday evenings to Saturday mornings. Admittedly, a survey shows that most members would prefer Saturday. But nearly all of our junior players have school sports on Saturday mornings and could not attend, while the members who prefer Saturday are all able to play on Tuesday evenings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: A club should schedule its events at whatever time the majority of its members prefer.
A schedule change that would keep some members from taking part should not be made merely to satisfy a preference of members who could take part under either schedule.
Club officers are not bound by the results of a survey of the club’s members.
Members who cannot attend an event because of other commitments should not have a say in when that event is held.
A club should survey its members before making any change to the schedule of its regular events.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the principle that takes the argument's facts and delivers its conclusion. The president's facts are that the move would shut out the junior players while the Saturday fans can play either day; B says exactly that such a change, made only to satisfy a preference, should not be made. The most tempting trap is C, because it seems to let the president set aside the survey; but freeing the officers from the survey doesn't tell them to keep Tuesday, so it doesn't justify the conclusion. A supports the opposite conclusion, and D would silence the juniors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The club should not move the tournament from Tuesday evening to Saturday morning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most members prefer Saturday (conceded); nearly all junior players couldn't attend on Saturday; everyone who prefers Saturday can still play on Tuesday.

breakdown.analysis: So most people prefer Saturday. Why isn't that the end of it? Because the president weighs a preference against being shut out. Moving the tournament would exclude the juniors just so others get the time they like better. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need: don't make a change that excludes some people just to satisfy the preference of people who can come either way. It's like refusing to move the family dinner to a time Grandma can't make just because the cousins would slightly rather eat later.

choices.note: Opposite. The majority prefers Saturday, so this principle would justify moving the tournament, not keeping it.

CORRECT. Moving to Saturday would keep the juniors from playing, and the only gain is a preference of members who can play on Tuesday anyway. This principle says don't make that change, which is the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like it lets the president ignore the survey. But being free to ignore a survey isn't a reason to keep Tuesday. It doesn't tell the club what to do, so it can't justify the conclusion.
Opposite. This would take away the juniors' say, since they're the ones who can't attend on Saturday. It works against the president's reasoning.
Irrelevant. The club already surveyed its members. A rule requiring a survey says nothing about whether to move the tournament.

questions.stimulus: Seed bank director: We add a seed sample to our permanent collection if, and only if, the sample passes a germination test and either belongs to an endangered species or comes from a population not yet represented in the collection.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The marsh orchid sample should be added to the permanent collection, since the marsh orchid is an endangered species.
The red clover sample passed its germination test, so it should be added to the permanent collection.
The dune grass sample comes from a population already represented in the collection, so it should not be added.
The wild oat sample passed its germination test but should not be added, since wild oat is not an endangered species.
The cliff fern sample should be added even though its population is already represented in the collection, since the cliff fern is endangered and the sample passed its germination test.
questions.explanation: Core move: an 'if and only if' rule with one required condition plus an either/or condition; the right judgment must establish both. E has the germination test passed and the endangered branch of the 'either/or' satisfied, so the sample must be added, and the already-represented population doesn't matter. The most tempting trap is A, which satisfies the either/or condition but says nothing about whether the orchid sample passed its germination test. C and D each rule out only one branch of the either/or, so the other branch could still qualify the sample.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Added ↔ (passes germination test) AND (endangered OR population not yet represented).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: To say 'add', the judgment must show the test was passed AND one branch of the 'or'. To say 'don't add', it must show the test failed OR both branches fail.

breakdown.analysis: Two requirements: the test, plus one of two qualifiers. Every trap gives you only part. For 'add,' check: 1. passed the test? 2. endangered or new population? For 'don't add,' you need a failed test, or BOTH qualifiers missing. Ruling out one branch of an 'or' proves nothing.

choices.note: Tempting. Endangered satisfies the 'or' part. But we don't know whether the orchid sample passed its germination test, and that's required. Half the rule isn't enough.
Missing the second requirement. Passing the test isn't enough; the sample also has to be endangered or from a new population. We're told neither.
Rules out only one branch. Dune grass might be endangered, in which case an already-represented population doesn't matter. We can't say 'don't add.'
Rules out only the other branch. Wild oat isn't endangered, but the sample might come from a population not yet represented. If so, it qualifies.
CORRECT. Passed the test: yes. Endangered: yes, which satisfies the 'or'. So the rule requires adding it, and 'already represented' doesn't matter once the endangered branch is met.

questions.stimulus: Transit official: The Ostrey Island ferry should not be replaced by the proposed bridge. Admittedly, the bridge would shorten the trip for nearly all travelers and would cost less to maintain than the ferry. But building it would require demolishing the island’s only harbor wall, and the island’s fishing fleet, which supports a third of the island’s households, cannot operate without that wall.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the transit official’s reasoning?
choices: Savings in travel time and maintenance costs cannot by themselves justify a project that would deprive a substantial share of a community’s households of their livelihood.
A transportation project that would benefit nearly all of a community’s travelers should be carried out unless it would deprive some residents of their livelihood.
A transportation project should be carried out only if it would benefit nearly all of the people who would use it.
When a ferry is replaced by a bridge, the people who worked on the ferry should be compensated for the loss of their jobs.
Decisions about public works on an island should be made by the island’s residents rather than by officials on the mainland.
questions.explanation: Core move: the justifying principle must lead to 'don't build,' and conditional traps that only permit or only require something won't. The bridge's only listed advantages are time and maintenance savings, and it would cost a third of the households their livelihood; A says those savings can't justify such a project, so the bridge should not replace the ferry. The strongest trap is B, which mentions lost livelihoods and so looks like a reason not to build; but 'should be carried out unless X' only says what to do when X is absent, so when X is present it yields no verdict at all. C gives a necessary condition the bridge appears to meet, so it can't yield 'don't build' either.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ferry should not be replaced by the bridge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Conceded: the bridge would shorten trips for nearly all travelers and cost less to maintain; but building it destroys the only harbor wall, without which the fishing fleet, supporting a third of households, can't operate.

breakdown.analysis: The official grants the bridge's benefits. So why not build it? Because it would wipe out the livelihood of a third of the island. The principle has to say: those benefits don't outweigh that harm, so don't build. Watch the conditional direction. 'Do X unless Y' tells you what happens when Y is absent. It says nothing when Y is present. It's like 'We'll picnic unless it rains': if it rains, we might still picnic indoors. 'Unless' rules: no harm → build. Harm → nothing follows.

choices.note: CORRECT. Indirectly phrased, but it's the one. The bridge's advantages are exactly time savings and lower maintenance, and it would take the livelihood of a third of the households. So those advantages can't justify it, which means the bridge shouldn't replace the ferry.

Tempting. It mentions lost livelihoods, so it looks like the reason not to build. But 'should be carried out unless it deprives residents of livelihood' means: no deprivation → build. When there IS deprivation, the rule is silent. It never says 'don't build.'
Wrong direction. 'Only if' gives a necessary condition: carried out → benefits nearly all users. The bridge seems to meet it. Meeting a necessary condition never tells you not to build.
Irrelevant. Ferry workers aren't mentioned, and a rule about compensation doesn't say whether to build the bridge.
Out of scope. Who decides isn't the issue. The official's argument is about what the right decision is.

questions.stimulus: Clinic director: No volunteer at our legal aid clinic may advise a client unless the volunteer is a licensed attorney. A licensed attorney may advise any client, except that an attorney who has not completed our tenant-law training may not advise a client in an eviction case unless a trained attorney reviews the advice before it is given.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the rules stated by the clinic director?
choices: Because Oduya is a licensed attorney, she was permitted to advise a client in an eviction case without having her advice reviewed.
Because Pell has completed the clinic’s tenant-law training, he was permitted to advise a client in an eviction case.
Hanley advised a client in an eviction case without having the advice reviewed, and in doing so did not violate the director’s rules; so Hanley must have completed the tenant-law training.
Because Marsh’s advice to a client in an eviction case was reviewed by a trained attorney before it was given, Marsh was permitted to give it.
Because Ibsen has not completed the tenant-law training, she was not permitted to advise a client in a dispute over a security deposit.
questions.explanation: Core move: run the rules backward. Anyone who gives unreviewed eviction advice without violating the rules must be licensed (rule 1) and, since there was no review, must not be an untrained attorney (rule 2), so Hanley must have completed the training (C). The most tempting trap is D, which nails the review requirement but forgets the first rule: only licensed attorneys may advise anyone, and we aren't told Marsh is one. B makes the same mistake from the other side, since training without a license permits nothing, and A ignores that Oduya may be untrained.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: 1. Advise anyone → licensed attorney. 2. Untrained attorney advising in an eviction case → advice reviewed first by a trained attorney. Contrapositive of 2: eviction advice given without review → the attorney is trained (or isn't allowed).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A 'permitted' judgment must show: licensed AND (not eviction OR trained OR reviewed). A 'must have' judgment must follow from the rules plus the stated facts.

breakdown.analysis: Two gates. Gate 1: are you licensed? Without that, nothing else matters. Gate 2 applies only to eviction cases: if you're untrained, your advice needs a trained attorney's review. Every trap clears one gate and forgets the other. Now run it backward: if someone gave unreviewed eviction advice and broke no rule, they passed gate 1 (licensed), and since there was no review, they must be trained. That's a contrapositive, and it's the kind of awkward answer the hardest questions hide behind.

choices.note: Licensed clears gate 1, but this is an eviction case with no review. That's only allowed if Oduya is trained, and we aren't told she is. 'Licensed' alone doesn't permit it.
Gate 2 is fine, since trained attorneys don't need review. But the rules never say training makes you a licensed attorney. If Pell isn't licensed, he can't advise anyone.
CORRECT. No violation means Hanley is licensed. Eviction case, no review: under rule 2 that's forbidden for an untrained attorney. So Hanley must be trained. This follows strictly from the rules.

Tempting, and the trap built to catch you. The review satisfies rule 2 for an untrained attorney. But rule 1 comes first: only licensed attorneys may advise anyone, and we don't know Marsh is licensed. Review doesn't make a nonattorney eligible. One missing word, 'licensed,' sinks it.
Wrong scope. A security-deposit dispute isn't an eviction case, so the training rule doesn't apply. If Ibsen is licensed, she may give this advice.

questions.stimulus: Every kite sold at Fenner’s shop is made of ripstop nylon, and every ripstop nylon kite comes with a one-year guarantee against tearing. So the kite Alma bought at Fenner’s shop comes with a one-year guarantee against tearing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every ferry on the Selby route stops at Penn Island, and some ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars. So the ferry Juno took on the Selby route carried cars.
Every play staged by the Linden Players is performed in the old granary, and every performance in the old granary is unamplified. So the play Tess saw the Linden Players stage was unamplified.
Every seed sample in the Hollin vault has been dried, and every dried sample has been tested for disease. So any sample that has been tested for disease is in the Hollin vault.
Every loom at the Abner mill is inspected monthly, and every loom that is inspected monthly runs reliably. So the Abner mill will not need to buy new looms this year.
No member of the chess club who plays in the spring tournament may skip the opening meeting, and Ren is a member of the chess club. So Ren will attend the opening meeting.
questions.explanation: Core move: match a simple chain, all A are B, all B are C, this item is an A, so it is C. B has exactly that: Linden play → granary → unamplified, and Tess saw a Linden play. The most tempting trap is A, which looks almost identical, but its second premise says only 'some' ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars, so the chain breaks. C reverses the chain, D concludes something the premises never mention, and E leaves out the needed fact that Ren plays in the tournament.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Alma's kite from Fenner's comes with a one-year tear guarantee.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Fenner's kite is ripstop nylon; every ripstop nylon kite has the guarantee; Alma's kite is from Fenner's.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; all B are C; this x is an A; so x is C. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: A clean chain: Fenner's → ripstop → guarantee. Alma's kite is a Fenner's kite, so it gets the guarantee. Find another 'all, all, this one, so' chain that runs the same direction. Check quantifiers: one 'some' in the middle breaks the whole chain.

choices.note: Tempting. Same shape on the surface. But 'some ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars' is not 'all.' Juno's ferry could be one that doesn't. The chain breaks at 'some.'
CORRECT. Linden play → granary → unamplified. Tess saw a Linden play, so it was unamplified. Same valid chain, same direction.
Reversed. The premises say vault → dried → tested. The conclusion runs tested → vault, which is backward. It also concludes about a whole group, not about one item.
New idea in the conclusion. The premises are about reliable looms; the conclusion jumps to buying new looms, which nothing connects.
Missing link. The rule applies to members who play in the spring tournament. We're only told Ren is a member, not that he's playing.

questions.stimulus: A ferry crossing can leave on time only if the loading crew arrives early. The loading crew arrived early this morning. So this morning’s crossing left on time.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: A play can open on schedule only if its set is finished. The set for the new play was not finished. So the new play did not open on schedule.
If an injured owl’s wing has healed, the owl can be released. This owl’s wing has not healed. So this owl cannot be released.
A seed sample is stored in the cold vault only if it has been dried. This sample is stored in the cold vault. So this sample has been dried.
A loom can run at full speed only if it has been oiled. The loom on the east floor was oiled today. So the loom on the east floor is running at full speed.
Whenever the chess club meets on a Friday, attendance rises. The club will meet on a Friday next week. So attendance will rise next week.
questions.explanation: Core move: diagnose the flaw, then find the same flaw. The argument treats a necessary condition (the crew arriving early) as if it were sufficient for leaving on time; D does the same with oiling and full speed. The most tempting trap is B, which is also a flawed conditional argument, but its error is different: it assumes that failing a sufficient condition (a healed wing) rules out the result. A, C, and E are valid arguments, so they can't match a flawed one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This morning's crossing left on time.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Leave on time → crew arrives early; the crew arrived early.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X only if Y; Y happened; so X. (Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' marks a requirement. On time → crew early. The crew showing up early means the crossing COULD leave on time; it doesn't mean it did. It's like saying 'you can pass only if you study; you studied, so you passed.' This is the necessary-versus-sufficient flaw. It's a classic; know it. Find the answer that meets a requirement and declares the result.

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match. Open on schedule → set finished. Set not finished, so not on schedule. That's the contrapositive, done correctly.

Tempting, because it's also a broken conditional. But it's a different break. Healed → can be released. Not healed, so can't be released: that denies the sufficient condition. The stimulus affirms the necessary condition instead. Same family, different flaw.
Valid. Cold vault → dried. In the cold vault, so dried. The arrow runs the right way.
CORRECT. Full speed → oiled. It was oiled, so it's at full speed. Same error: a requirement is met and the result is assumed to follow.
Valid. Friday → attendance rises. Next week is a Friday meeting, so attendance rises. The sufficient condition is met, so the result does follow.

questions.stimulus: The Brisk Valley seed bank will extend its opening hours only if it receives a state grant, and it will receive a state grant only if it hires a second archivist. Since the seed bank has decided not to hire a second archivist, it will not extend its opening hours.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The Elm Street Theater will add a Sunday matinee only if its lead actor agrees to it, and she will agree only if she is paid extra. Since the theater cannot pay her extra, it will not add a Sunday matinee.
The Harlan ferry will add a late sailing only if demand rises, and demand will rise only if fares are cut. Since fares are being cut, the ferry will add a late sailing.

The chess club will move to a larger hall if its membership grows, and its membership will grow if it offers a course for beginners. Since the club is offering a beginners’ course, it will move to a larger hall.
Tolland Airport will expand its terminal only if passenger numbers grow and the county approves funding. Since the county has approved funding, the airport will expand its terminal.
The Calder mill will reopen its dye house only if it wins a new contract. Since it will not win a new contract, it will not hire any new workers.
questions.explanation: Core move: map the chain and the direction of inference. The stimulus links hours → grant → archivist and then denies the last link to deny the first; A does exactly that with matinee → actor agrees → extra pay. The strongest trap is C, which is also a valid chain, but it runs forward from a sufficient condition to its result rather than backward by denying a requirement, so its pattern differs. B and D affirm necessary conditions, which is invalid, and E's conclusion introduces hiring, which the premise never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seed bank will not extend its hours.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Extend hours → grant; grant → second archivist; no second archivist.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A. (Valid: a chain run backward through the contrapositive.)

breakdown.analysis: Chain: hours → grant → archivist. No archivist, so no grant, so no extended hours. That's the contrapositive run all the way back. A valid argument needs a valid match, and the same direction matters: this one denies the last requirement to deny the first thing. It's like: 'You'll get the job only if you interview, and you'll interview only if you apply. You didn't apply, so no job.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Matinee → actor agrees → paid extra. Can't pay extra, so she won't agree, so no matinee. Same chain, same backward direction.

Invalid. Late sailing → demand → fare cut. Fares are being cut, which only meets a requirement. It concludes the sailing will be added, which affirms a necessary condition. The stimulus is valid; this isn't.

Tempting. It's a valid two-step chain, so it feels like a match. But it runs forward: course → growth → larger hall, and the course is happening. The stimulus runs backward, denying the final requirement. Valid isn't enough; the pattern must match.
Invalid, and the structure differs. One requirement has two parts (growth AND funding), and only one part is met. Meeting part of a necessary condition proves nothing.
The conclusion is about hiring workers, but the premise is only about reopening the dye house. The conclusion doesn't connect to the premise at all.

questions.stimulus: Most members of the Glenmore Chess Club play in the club’s Thursday league, and most players in the Thursday league are under thirty years old. So most members of the Glenmore Chess Club are under thirty years old.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most passengers on the Selby ferry buy return tickets, and most passengers on the Selby ferry are island residents. So some island residents who ride the Selby ferry buy return tickets.
Most of the Abner mill’s weavers work the night shift, and most of the mill’s night-shift workers are union members. So most of the mill’s union members are weavers.
Most kites sold at Pell’s shop are box kites, and all box kites sold at Pell’s shop are handmade. So most kites sold at Pell’s shop are handmade.
Most of the owls admitted to the Fenwick wildlife center have wing injuries. So most owls with wing injuries are admitted to the Fenwick wildlife center.
Most flights at Tolland Airport are operated by Skyline Air, and most Skyline Air flights at Tolland depart before noon. So most flights at Tolland Airport depart before noon.
questions.explanation: Core move: 'most A are B, and most B are C, so most A are C' is invalid, because the B's that are C and the A's that are B need not be the same ones. E repeats that exact pattern with flights, Skyline flights, and morning departures. The most tempting trap is C, which looks identical but uses 'all' in the second premise, which makes it valid; A is also valid, since two 'most' statements about the same group guarantee some overlap. B and D are flawed, but they reverse a claim rather than chaining two 'most' statements.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most club members are under thirty.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most members play in the Thursday league; most Thursday-league players are under thirty.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C. (Invalid: 'most' doesn't chain.)

breakdown.analysis: Can you chain 'most' with 'most'? No. Picture 100 members, 60 of them in the league. 'Most league players are under thirty' could mean just 31 of those 60. The other 40 members could all be older. That's 31 out of 100, not most. 'Most' isn't 'all': the members you care about could be the other ones. Find the same broken chain. Watch for lookalikes that swap in 'all' (which fixes it) or that compare two 'most' claims about the same group (which is valid for 'some').

choices.note: Tempting, but valid. Two 'most' statements about the SAME group (Selby passengers) must overlap: more than half plus more than half is more than all. So some residents buy return tickets. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Flawed, but differently. The conclusion flips the direction (most union members are weavers), which reverses a 'most' claim. The stimulus chains forward; this one turns around.

Tempting, because it's nearly word-for-word the same shape. But the second premise says ALL box kites are handmade, and that makes it valid: most kites are box kites, all of those are handmade, so most kites are handmade. One quantifier changes everything.
Flawed, but it's a simple reversal of one 'most' statement, not a chain of two. Different error.
CORRECT. Most flights are Skyline; most Skyline flights leave before noon; so most flights leave before noon. Same broken 'most + most' chain. The non-Skyline flights could all leave after noon.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife center director: Only people who have completed our bird-handling course are permitted to volunteer at the center, and every one of our volunteers is skilled at calming injured birds. It follows that anyone who has completed our bird-handling course is skilled at calming injured birds.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Everyone who volunteers at the Elm Street Theater must attend a safety briefing, and Halla has not attended a safety briefing. It follows that Halla does not volunteer at the Elm Street Theater.

Only students who pass the qualifying exam may join the Holt chess team, and every student who passes the qualifying exam has a rating above 1500. It follows that every member of the Holt chess team has a rating above 1500.

Every member of the Pell Street kite club owns at least one handmade kite, and no one may join the club without first attending a kite-making workshop. It follows that no one who has attended a kite-making workshop is without a handmade kite.
Every pilot based at Tolland Airport is certified for night flying, and Ines is certified for night flying. It follows that Ines must be a pilot based at Tolland Airport.

All of the Abner mill’s dyers wear respirators at work, and all of the mill’s dyers have completed its safety course. It follows that some people who have completed the mill’s safety course wear respirators at work.
questions.explanation: Core move: the director has two facts that are each necessary for volunteering (the course, and calming skill) and wrongly concludes that one guarantees the other: course → skilled. C has the same structure in disguise, with its premises in the opposite order and its conclusion stated as a double negative: club member → handmade kite, club member → workshop, so workshop → handmade kite. The most tempting trap is B, which shares the wording 'only students who pass … may join,' but its second premise links the requirement to the property directly, so it is a valid chain. D is a related but different error (inferring membership from a single necessary condition), and A and E are valid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Anyone who completed the bird-handling course is skilled at calming injured birds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Volunteer → completed course; volunteer → skilled at calming birds.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All M are A (A is required for M); all M are B; so all A are B. (Treats a requirement for membership as if it guaranteed what members have.)

breakdown.analysis: Volunteers took the course. Volunteers are skilled. So everyone who took the course is skilled? Plenty of people could take the course, never volunteer, and be hopeless with birds. The course is necessary for volunteering, not sufficient. It's like: 'Only people with a license may drive for us, and all our drivers are excellent, so everyone with a license is an excellent driver.' Now hunt for the same skeleton. It may be scrambled: premises swapped, conclusion phrased as 'no one ... is without.'

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match. Volunteer → briefing; Halla had no briefing; so she doesn't volunteer. A correct contrapositive.

Tempting. It even opens with 'Only students who pass ... may join,' just like the stimulus. But the second premise is about everyone who PASSES, not about members: join → pass → rating above 1500. That chain is valid. Same words, different logic.

CORRECT. Translate: member → handmade kite; member → attended workshop. Conclusion: 'no one who attended a workshop is without a handmade kite' = workshop → handmade kite. Two necessary conditions for membership, and one is treated as guaranteeing the other. Same flaw, just reordered and phrased negatively.

Flawed, but a different flaw. It infers that Ines is a member (a Tolland pilot) from one necessary condition. The stimulus never concludes that anyone is a member; it concludes that one requirement guarantees another trait.
Valid. If all dyers both wear respirators and took the course, then those dyers are people who took the course and wear respirators. It concludes only 'some,' which follows.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Fernley should restore the evening run of its harbor ferry. When the run was cut two years ago, the savings to the ferry service turned out to be small, while shops near the harbor reported that their evening customers fell by nearly half. Restoring the run would cost the town little and would help those shops recover.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Cutting the evening ferry run saved the ferry service only a small amount of money.
Shops near the harbor lost nearly half of their evening customers after the evening run was cut.
The ferry service should not have cut its evening run two years ago.
Restoring the evening ferry run would help the harbor shops recover.
Fernley should restore the evening run of its harbor ferry.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim everything else supports. The small savings, the shops' losses, and the low cost of restoring the run are all reasons for the recommendation in the first sentence, so E is the conclusion. The most tempting trap is C, which sounds like the council member's view, but she never says the original cut was a mistake; she argues about what to do now. A, B, and D are premises offered in support of E.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fernley should restore the evening ferry run.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The cut saved little; harbor shops lost nearly half their evening customers; restoring the run would cost little and help the shops recover.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Small savings, lost customers, cheap to restore: why tell us all that? To show that Fernley should bring the run back. Here the conclusion comes first, which is common. Don't assume it's the last sentence.

choices.note: Premise. This is one reason to restore the run, not the point being argued for.
Premise. The shops' losses support restoring the run. They aren't the conclusion.
Tempting. It sounds like what the council member believes. But she never says the cut was a mistake back then. She argues about what to do now. A conclusion about the past isn't her conclusion.
Premise. Helping the shops is a reason for restoring the run, given in the last sentence. It supports the recommendation; it isn't the recommendation.
CORRECT. Every other statement is a reason to do this. It's the recommendation the argument exists to support.

questions.stimulus: Theater director: Some board members want the Riverside Community Theater to stage only well-known musicals, on the grounds that familiar titles sell more tickets. But last season our two original plays sold nearly as many tickets as our musicals did, and the plays cost far less to produce. So the theater should keep staging original plays alongside its musicals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that familiar titles sell more tickets?
choices: It is the conclusion that the argument as a whole is intended to support.
It is a premise offered in support of the argument’s main conclusion.
It is a consideration offered in support of a proposal that the argument opposes.
It is evidence that the argument uses to show that the board members’ proposal would be costly.
It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the evidence about last season’s ticket sales.
questions.explanation: Core move: separate the author's own reasoning from the reasoning of the view the author rejects. The claim about familiar titles is the board members' reason for staging only musicals, a proposal the director argues against, so C is right. The most tempting trap is B, because the claim appears among the argument's premises; but it supports the board members' position, not the director's conclusion that original plays should stay. E fails because the director's ticket evidence pushes against that claim rather than establishing it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The theater should keep staging original plays alongside musicals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Opposing view: stage only well-known musicals, since familiar titles sell more tickets; but the original plays sold nearly as many tickets and cost far less to produce.

breakdown.analysis: Whose claim is this? Not the director's. It's the reason the board members give for their proposal. The director then pushes back with ticket and cost numbers. So the claim supports a view the director rejects. Watch for 'on the grounds that': it tells you you're hearing the other side's reasoning.

choices.note: No. The conclusion is that the theater should keep staging original plays, the last sentence. This claim is a reason for the opposite proposal.
Tempting, because the claim really is a premise for some conclusion. But for which one? It supports the board members' 'only musicals' proposal, not the director's conclusion. Wrong side.
CORRECT. 'Familiar titles sell more tickets' is the board members' reason for staging only musicals, and the director argues against that proposal.
No. The director's cost point is that original plays are cheaper. This claim is about ticket sales, and the director doesn't use it to show anything about the board members' proposal.
No. The ticket evidence cuts against this claim. The director uses it to show original plays sell nearly as well. Nothing is concluded from that evidence that familiar titles sell more.

questions.stimulus: Some textile historians claim that the Callan mill closed in 1912 because cheap imported cloth had driven down demand for its products. But the mill’s ledgers show that it received more orders in its final year than in any earlier year. The ledgers also record that the mill’s waterwheel was destroyed by a flood that spring and was never rebuilt. So the closure was most likely caused by the loss of the mill’s power source.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that because one proposed cause of an event cannot be confirmed, the event probably had no single cause
citing evidence that conflicts with a proposed explanation and offering an alternative explanation that fits the evidence
showing that the evidence on which the historians’ explanation rests is unreliable
conceding that imported cloth hurt the mill’s business but denying that it was severe enough to cause the closure
drawing a general conclusion about textile mills from the history of a single mill
questions.explanation: Core move: describe the argument's moves abstractly. It cites a record level of orders, which conflicts with the falling-demand explanation, and then offers the destroyed waterwheel as a better explanation, so B is right. The most tempting trap is D, because the argument does deny that imports caused the closure; but it never concedes that imported cloth hurt the mill at all, and its evidence suggests demand was strong. C fails because the argument attacks the historians' conclusion with new evidence, not the reliability of their evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Callan mill's closure was most likely caused by the loss of its waterwheel.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Historians say falling demand from cheap imports caused it; but orders were at a record high in the final year; and a flood destroyed the waterwheel that spring and it was never rebuilt.

breakdown.analysis: Two moves. 1. Knock down the historians' explanation: if demand had collapsed, why were orders at a record high? 2. Offer a better one: the mill lost its power. That's the classic 'evidence against their cause, plus my alternative cause.' It's like: 'You say the restaurant closed for lack of customers, but it had a waiting list every night. It closed because the kitchen burned down.' Find the answer that describes both moves.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument doesn't say the historians' cause just can't be confirmed, and it doesn't conclude there was no single cause. It names one cause.
choices.example: Example of method: No one can confirm that the storm caused the bridge to collapse, so the collapse probably resulted from many factors together.

choices.note: CORRECT. Record orders conflict with the falling-demand explanation; the destroyed waterwheel is an alternative explanation that fits the facts. Both moves described.

Tempting, since the argument does undercut the historians. But it never says their evidence is unreliable. We aren't even told what their evidence was. The argument brings in new evidence that conflicts with their conclusion.
choices.example: Example of method: The historians rely on a trade report that was later shown to contain invented figures, so their account can't be trusted.

choices.note: Tempting, because the argument does deny that imports caused the closure. But it never concedes imports hurt the mill. Record orders suggest business was strong. Don't read in a concession that isn't there.
choices.example: Example of method: Admittedly, cheap imports cut into the mill's sales, but the losses were too small to force it to close.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument is about one mill and draws a conclusion only about that mill.
choices.example: Example of method: The Callan mill closed after losing its waterwheel, so most textile mills of that era must have closed for lack of power.

questions.stimulus: Seed bank administrator: Critics call our plan to keep duplicate samples at a second site a waste of money, pointing out that our main vault has not lost a single sample in sixty years. The plan is admittedly expensive, but the critics are mistaken. A clean record shows little about how vulnerable a vault is if the vault has never faced the threat it is least able to withstand, and ours has never been through a prolonged power outage, the event most likely to destroy a collection all at once.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The main vault’s sixty-year record without losing a sample provides little evidence about how vulnerable the vault is.
A prolonged power outage is the event most likely to destroy a seed bank’s collection all at once.
The plan to keep duplicate samples at a second site is more expensive than the critics acknowledge.
Keeping duplicate samples at a second site is not a waste of money, even though the plan is expensive.
The seed bank should not rely on its main vault to protect any of its samples.
questions.explanation: Core move: find a conclusion that sits mid-argument and is stated only as 'the critics are mistaken,' then translate it. The critics say the duplicate-site plan is a waste of money, so saying they are mistaken means the plan is not a waste, which is D; the rest of the argument supports that. The strongest trap is A, which is a real conclusion of the argument, but an intermediate one: the point about the clean record is given as the reason the critics are mistaken. B is a premise, C distorts the concession, and E goes far beyond anything the administrator claims.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics are mistaken: keeping duplicates at a second site is not a waste of money (even though it's expensive).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. A clean record says little about vulnerability if the vault hasn't faced the threat it's least able to withstand; 2. our vault has never had a prolonged power outage, the event most likely to destroy a collection at once; so (intermediate) our sixty-year record shows little.

breakdown.analysis: The first sentence is the critics' view; the conclusion hides in the middle: 'the critics are mistaken.' Mistaken about what? That the plan is a waste. So the conclusion is: the plan is not a waste. Ask which statement supports which. 'Our clean record shows little' supports 'the critics are wrong,' not the other way around. That makes the record point an intermediate conclusion. Expect the right answer to be a translation, and expect the intermediate conclusion as the trap.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the main trap. It IS a conclusion, drawn from the general claim and the fact about power outages. But why does the administrator establish it? To show the critics are wrong about the plan. It supports the main point, so it's intermediate.
Premise. It's a fact offered in support, the last piece of evidence.
Distortion. The administrator concedes the plan is expensive, but never says the critics underestimate the cost.
CORRECT. 'The critics are mistaken' means the plan isn't a waste of money. The concession ('admittedly expensive') is folded in. Everything else in the argument supports this.
Too strong. The administrator wants a backup site, not to abandon the main vault for every sample.

questions.stimulus: Airport director: Some residents blame the new night-flight curfew at Harwick Regional Airport for the drop in hotel bookings in town, since bookings began falling the very month the curfew took effect. But if that timing were enough, we would also have to blame the curfew for the closing of the town’s only cinema that same month, and no one does. Moreover, bookings fell that month at hotels throughout the region, including in towns whose airports have no curfew. The decline is better explained by something affecting the whole region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that we would also have to blame the curfew for the closing of the town’s only cinema?
choices: It describes an implication of the residents’ reasoning that the director takes to be unacceptable.
It is offered as evidence that the decline in hotel bookings had a cause other than the curfew.
It is a claim that the director concedes is true but argues does not bear on the main conclusion.
It is an intermediate conclusion offered in support of the claim that the decline is better explained by a regional factor.
It is presented as an example of an event that, like the decline in bookings, resulted from something affecting the whole region.
questions.explanation: Core move: recognize a claim the author does not believe. The director says that if timing alone proved causation, the curfew would also have to be blamed for the cinema closing, 'and no one does'; it is an absurd consequence used to show the residents' reasoning proves too much, so A is right. The most tempting trap is B, because the claim does help defeat the residents; but it attacks only their inference, and it is the regional decline, not the cinema, that is evidence of a different cause. D fails because the cinema point is not a conclusion the director supports and then builds on; it is a consequence the director rejects.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in hotel bookings is better explained by something affecting the whole region (not the curfew).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Residents infer the curfew caused the drop from timing alone; that reasoning would also blame the curfew for the cinema closing, which no one accepts; bookings fell across the region, even where airports have no curfew.

breakdown.analysis: Does the director think the curfew closed the cinema? No. That's the point. The author doesn't believe this. It's the absurd result used to sink the residents' reasoning: 'if timing alone proved cause, you'd have to say this too, and that's silly.' Notice what it does and doesn't do. It shows the timing argument is weak. It does NOT show some other cause is at work. That job belongs to the regional evidence. It's like answering 'the rooster crowed and then the sun rose, so the rooster raised the sun.'

choices.note: CORRECT. The cinema point follows from the residents' 'timing is enough' reasoning, and the director rejects it ('no one does'). It's an unacceptable implication used to discredit that reasoning.

Tempting, because it does help knock out the curfew explanation. But it attacks only the residents' inference. Showing an argument proves too much doesn't show the effect had another cause. Evidence of another cause comes from the regional decline, the next sentence.
No. The director doesn't concede that the curfew closed the cinema; the whole point is that no one believes it. And the claim does bear on the argument: it undercuts the residents.

Tempting at a glance, but the director never supports this claim with evidence and never uses it as a step toward the regional explanation. It's a consequence the director rejects, not a conclusion the director draws.
Misreads the argument. Nothing says the cinema closed because of a regional factor. The cinema is mentioned only to show where the residents' reasoning would lead.

passages.title: Cooperative Grain Elevators on the Carlin Plains
passages.text:
Between 1900 and 1920, farmers in the Carlin Plains region built more than two hundred cooperative grain elevators: tall wooden storehouses beside the railroad tracks where grain was weighed, graded, and loaded onto freight cars. Before the cooperatives appeared, most elevators in the region were owned by a few 'line' companies, each operating dozens of elevators along a railroad. Farmers had long complained that these companies graded their grain unfairly low and paid less than it was worth, and historians have usually explained the spread of the cooperatives as the farmers' response to these grievances.

The historian Ada Reinholt has argued that this explanation is incomplete. Grievances against the line companies, she points out, were widespread long before 1900, and several cooperatives founded in the 1890s failed within a few years. What changed after 1900, in Reinholt's account, was not the farmers' anger but their means of acting on it. Two developments were crucial. First, a 1903 law required the railroads to provide track space to any elevator meeting basic standards, ending a practice in which railroads, at the line companies' urging, had refused sidings to cooperatives. Second, the founding of a regional cooperative sales agency in 1905 gave small local cooperatives access to buyers in distant markets, which they had been unable to reach on their own.

Reinholt supports her account with records of where and when cooperatives were founded. In the two years after the 1903 law, new cooperatives appeared at nearly four times the rate of the preceding decade, and they clustered in towns along the rail lines that had most often refused sidings in the past. Cooperatives in towns that joined the sales agency, moreover, were far more likely than others to remain in operation for a decade or more. The line companies' grading practices, by contrast, changed little over the same period.

Reinholt's emphasis on law and organization is a valuable corrective, and her evidence about timing is difficult to dispute. Yet in one respect her account may lean too far in the other direction. A track-space law and a sales agency made cooperatives possible; they did not make farmers willing to invest their scarce savings in them. Local newspapers from the period suggest that a cooperative was often founded soon after a particular grievance, such as a disputed grading or a sudden cut in prices, galvanized a community. The grievances that Reinholt treats as a constant background may thus have supplied the occasion for founding a given cooperative, even if new laws and institutions explain why such efforts now succeeded where earlier ones had failed.

passages.title: The Reused Blocks of Teodora Halm
passages.text:
The woodcut prints of Teodora Halm, made in the 1920s and 1930s in the market town of Vesk, have long puzzled collectors. Many of them show faint, ghostly lines, such as a fragment of a roofline or the curve of a face, that bear no relation to the image in which they appear. Halm cut her images into blocks of pearwood, and it is now known that she reused the same blocks repeatedly, planing away an old image and cutting a new one into the fresh surface. (A woodcut prints from the raised surface that remains after the artist cuts away everything meant to stay blank.) Because the planing was often shallow, traces of the earlier image sometimes survived and printed along with the new one.

For decades, critics regarded these traces as accidents of poverty. Halm, they noted, sold her prints cheaply at the Vesk market and could rarely afford new wood; the ghostly lines were thus flaws she tolerated rather than effects she sought. On this view, the most valuable impressions are the cleanest ones, and several museum catalogs have described prints with prominent traces as 'compromised.'

The art historian Jonas Remmet has recently argued that this judgment misreads Halm's practice. Remmet observes that Halm's account books show that she bought new pearwood at least twice a year, even in her leanest periods, yet she went on planing and recutting her oldest blocks. More tellingly, the traces are not randomly distributed. In a series of market scenes from 1931, the faint outline of the town's demolished grain hall appears behind the stalls in print after print, positioned with evident care. Remmet concludes that Halm came to use the traces deliberately, as a way of letting the town's past show through its present.

Remmet's argument is strongest where it rests on the 1931 series, in which the placement of the traces is difficult to explain as accident. It is weaker as an account of Halm's work as a whole. Many earlier prints carry traces that seem to have no connection to the subjects of their images, some of them cutting awkwardly across a figure's face, and Halm's letters, which discuss her methods at length, never mention the traces at all. The likeliest story is that a technical necessity gradually became an artistic resource: Halm began by tolerating the traces and ended by composing with them. If so, the catalogers' habit of ranking impressions by their cleanness is mistaken, not because every trace is intentional, but because some are, and no single standard of value can be applied across her entire career.

passages.title: Handwriting Experts in the Courts of Tarland
passages.text:
In the province of Tarland, a witness may give expert testimony comparing a disputed document with samples of a person's known handwriting if the court finds the witness qualified 'by knowledge, skill, training, or experience.' Tarland's courts have interpreted this standard generously. A witness who has worked for some years as a document examiner, and who can describe the features examiners compare, such as letter proportions, the slant and pressure of strokes, and the ways letters are joined, is ordinarily permitted to testify and to tell the jury whether, in the witness's opinion, the defendant wrote the document in question. Opposing counsel may cross-examine such a witness, but challenges to the admissibility of the testimony itself rarely succeed.

The legal scholar Mirela Vasko argues that this standard asks the wrong question. Whether a witness is experienced, she observes, says nothing about whether the comparisons the witness performs actually distinguish one writer from another. An experienced practitioner of an unreliable technique is not thereby made reliable; experience may simply make the practitioner more confident. Vasko proposes that Tarland's courts admit handwriting testimony only from examiners who have passed blind proficiency tests, in which examiners compare samples whose true authorship is known to the test's designers but not to the examiners, and that each examiner's error rate on those tests be disclosed to the jury.

Vasko's critique is well founded, and her proposal would be a considerable improvement on current practice. A 2011 study commissioned by Tarland's bar association found that examiners who had testified in Tarland's courts reached conflicting conclusions in nearly a fifth of the test comparisons they were given, yet each of them had been admitted on the strength of experience alone. A standard that cannot screen out disagreement on that scale is not doing the work an admissibility standard exists to do.

Still, proficiency testing addresses only part of the difficulty. An error rate measured on test samples describes how an examiner performs on the kinds of comparisons the test contains. Disputed documents in actual cases, however, often involve brief signatures, deliberately disguised writing, or writers whose hand has changed with age, conditions under which an examiner who performs well on ordinary samples may perform far worse. A low error rate disclosed to a jury could thus lend an examiner's opinion in a difficult case more weight than it deserves. Vasko's proposal would be strengthened by requiring that proficiency tests include comparisons resembling the one at issue in the case or, where no such tests exist, that the examiner be limited to describing the similarities and differences between the samples without offering an opinion on who wrote the document.

passages.title: Kin Recognition in the Roots of Carrowa
passages.text:
When two plants of the coastal annual Carrowa littoralis share a pot, each typically invests more of its biomass in roots than a plant grown alone, a response ecologists interpret as competition for soil nutrients, since a plant with more roots captures a larger share of a limited supply. In 2009 the botanist Ines Valdt reported a twist: the increase was much smaller when the two plants grew from seeds of the same mother plant than when they grew from seeds of different mothers. Valdt proposed that Carrowa recognizes kin through chemical cues released by roots and restrains its competitive investment when its neighbor is a relative, a restraint that would benefit the plant's genes, many of which its siblings share.

The proposal met immediate resistance. Critics noted that siblings resemble one another not only in their genes but also in their size and rate of growth, since they develop from seeds provisioned by the same parent. Two plants of similar size, the critics argued, may simply compete on more equal terms, so that neither is pushed into the steep root investment that a smaller plant makes when it finds itself beside a larger one. On this account, the pattern Valdt observed would arise from size matching, with no recognition involved. Valdt's original pairs, they pointed out, had not been matched for size.

Valdt responded with experiments designed to separate the two explanations. First she paired siblings and nonsiblings that had been matched for seed weight and early growth, and found that the difference in root allocation persisted. She then grew plants singly in soil that had previously held either a sibling or a stranger, with the earlier plant's roots removed but any compounds they had secreted left in place. Plants in stranger-conditioned soil produced more roots than those in sibling-conditioned soil, though the difference was only about half as large as in the paired trials.

These results make size matching an unlikely explanation for the effect, but they leave the recognition hypothesis less complete than Valdt sometimes suggests. That conditioned soil reproduced only part of the response implies that root secretions, though they evidently carry some information about a neighbor's identity, are not the whole mechanism; contact between living roots, or cues that degrade soon after a plant is removed, may account for the remainder. Nor do the experiments show that restraint toward siblings actually benefits a plant's genes. A plant that grows fewer roots beside a sibling might leave nutrients for the sibling to capture, but it might equally leave them unused, and only a comparison of the combined seed production of sibling and nonsibling pairs could tell which.

passages.title: Filling Losses in Medieval Wall Paintings
passages.text:
When a medieval wall painting has lost patches of its paint layer, through damp, flaking, or the careless removal of later plaster, a conservator must decide what, if anything, to put in the gaps. Few conservators today would repaint the missing areas in imitation of the original, a once-common practice now generally rejected because it passes off a modern conjecture as medieval work. The live dispute concerns the gentler alternatives. Some conservators favor fills that reconstruct the missing image in a technique detectable on close inspection, such as tratteggio, in which the fill is built up from fine parallel strokes that merge with the surrounding image at a distance but reveal themselves up close. Others hold that losses should be left as bare plaster or toned in a single neutral color, so that nothing is added that the painter did not put there.

The conservator Ilse Brandvold, defending the second position in her treatment of the chapel at Sankt Orm, has argued that distinguishability is a weaker safeguard than its advocates suppose. A fill that can be told from the original only by a viewer who stands close and looks for it is, for the great majority of visitors, simply part of the picture. What such fills protect, she contends, is the conservator's honesty, not the viewer's understanding.

Her opponents reply that bare losses do damage of their own. A large gap near the center of a composition does not present itself to the eye as an absence; it reads as a shape, often the most prominent shape on the wall, so that the viewer's attention is drawn to precisely the part of the painting that no longer exists. Leaving a loss bare, on this view, is not abstaining from interpretation but substituting one distortion for another.

Each side is right about the other and wrong about itself. Brandvold's objection to tratteggio holds wherever a fill must supply something the surviving fragments do not determine, such as a face whose features are wholly lost, because there even a distinguishable fill presents the conservator's invention with the authority of the image around it. But where a loss interrupts a pattern or a fold whose course is fixed by what survives on either side, a fill adds nothing that the painting itself does not already state, and Brandvold's worry lapses. Her opponents' point about bare losses, conversely, is strongest for exactly these small, determinate gaps, and weakest for the large ones, where any fill would have to invent. The question, then, is not which treatment is more honest in general but whether a given loss is one that the surviving painting can itself fill.
